translations.en-GB: Where is there a pharmacy nearby?

mnemonic.title: Pharmacy with an f
mnemonic.text: «Farmacia» is “pharmacy” spelt the Spanish way: ph becomes f, as in «foto» and «teléfono».

grammar.title: «Hay» for any one
grammar.text: «Hay» (there is) goes with «una»: any pharmacy at all. For a particular one, use «está»: «¿Dónde está la farmacia?».

pronunciation.title: «Hay» sounds like “eye”
pronunciation.text: «Hay» sounds just like English “eye”: the h is silent.

phrases.target: ¿Tiene algo para el dolor de cabeza?

translations.en-GB: Do you have something for a headache?
translations.ru-RU: У вас есть что-нибудь от головной боли?

mnemonic.title: A cabbage for a head
mnemonic.text: «Cabeza» (head) sounds like “cabbage”, and a cabbage is a head: picture one with a headache, «dolor de cabeza».

grammar.title: «Para» says what it's for
grammar.text: «Para» says what something is for: «algo para el dolor», something for the pain. «Tiene» is the polite usted form.

pronunciation.title: Castilian z in cabeza
pronunciation.ipa: [ˈtje.ne ˈal.ɣo ˈpa.ɾa el doˈloɾ ðe kaˈβe.θa]
pronunciation.respelling: TYEH-neh AHL-goh PAH-rah el doh-LOR deh kah-BEH-thah
pronunciation.text: In Spain the z of «cabeza» sounds like the th in “think”.

mnemonic.title: Gargle with garganta
mnemonic.text: «Garganta» (throat) starts like “gargle”, which is just what you do with a sore one.

grammar.title: The throat does the hurting
grammar.text: The throat is the subject: «me duele la garganta», literally “the throat hurts me”. Plural: «me duelen los pies». Body parts take «la», not «mi».

pronunciation.title: One syllable: due
pronunciation.text: «Due» in «duele» is one syllable, “dweh”, and it carries the stress.

translations.en-GB: I need to see a doctor

mnemonic.title: Médico, like medic
mnemonic.text: «Médico» is the everyday word for a doctor, like “medic”. «Doctor» is heard too, often as a title: «el doctor García».

grammar.title: The personal «a»
grammar.text: A person as the object takes «a»: «ver a un médico». A thing doesn't: «ver la catedral».

pronunciation.title: MÉ-di-co
pronunciation.text: The accent mark puts the stress on the first syllable: «MÉ-di-co», never “meh-DEE-koh”.

mnemonic.title: Two easy cognates
mnemonic.text: Both words are English in Spanish spelling: allergy → «alergia», penicillin → «penicilina».

grammar.title: Having an allergy
grammar.text: Spanish “has” an allergy: «tengo alergia a…», with «a» before the cause. Or say «soy alérgico a…» («alérgica» for a woman).

pronunciation.title: ci as “thee”
pronunciation.text: In Spain «ci» in «penicilina» is said with the th of “think”: peh-nee-thee-LEE-nah.

translations.en-GB: How often do I take it?

mnemonic.title: Cada, on the beat
mnemonic.text: «Cada» (every) sounds like “cadence”, a steady beat: «cada ocho horas», every eight hours, like clockwork.

grammar.title: «Cuánto» agrees
grammar.text: «Cuánto» agrees with its noun: «cuántas horas» (feminine plural), «cuántos días». «Lo» stands for the medicine.

pronunciation.title: The “kw” in cuántas
pronunciation.text: «Cuán» sounds like “kwahn”, and the accent mark shows where the stress falls.

phrases.target: Tengo una reserva a nombre de García

translations.en-GB: I have a booking under the name García
translations.bg-BG: Имам резервация на името на Гарсия
translations.ru-RU: У меня бронь на имя Гарсия

mnemonic.title: Held in reserve
mnemonic.text: «Reserva» is something held in reserve: picture a room the hotel keeps in reserve just for García.

grammar.title: «A nombre de»
grammar.text: «A nombre de» means “in the name of”. The surname follows with no article: «a nombre de García».

pronunciation.title: Initial r is rolled
pronunciation.ipa: [ˈteŋ.ɡo ˈu.na reˈseɾ.βa a ˈnom.bɾe ðe ɣaɾˈθi.a]
pronunciation.respelling: TENG-goh OO-nah reh-SEHR-vah ah NOM-breh deh gar-THEE-ah
pronunciation.text: An r at the start of a word is rolled, like rr: «reserva». The r in the middle is a single tap.

mnemonic.title: Break-fast
mnemonic.text: «Ayuno» means a fast, and «des-» undoes it: «desayuno» is literally “break-fast”, just like the English.

grammar.title: «A» with clock times
grammar.text: «¿A qué hora…?» asks at what time. The answer keeps the «a»: «a las ocho», at eight.

pronunciation.title: Qu sounds like k
pronunciation.respelling: ah KEH OH-rah es el deh-sah-YOO-noh
pronunciation.text: In «qué» the u is silent: it sounds like “keh”.

mnemonic.title: Toalla sounds like towel
mnemonic.text: «Toalla» sounds a lot like “towel”: toh-AH-yah. A bath towel is a «toalla de baño».

grammar.title: Polite «puede»
grammar.text: «¿Me puede…?» + infinitive is a polite request to usted. «Me» can also go on the end: «¿Puede darme otra toalla?».

pronunciation.title: Three syllables: to-a-lla
pronunciation.text: Say every vowel: «toalla» is «to-A-lla», three syllables, with the stress on the a.

mnemonic.title: Air that won’t function
mnemonic.text: «Aire acondicionado» is “air conditioned”, almost letter for letter, and «no funciona» is “doesn’t function”: picture the air itself refusing to work.

grammar.title: «No» before the verb
grammar.text: Spanish makes a verb negative with «no» in front, with no “doesn't”: «funciona» → «no funciona».

pronunciation.title: Ai sounds like “eye”
pronunciation.text: «Ai» in «aire» sounds like “eye”, and the r after it is one quick tap.

translations.en-GB: Can I leave my bags here?
translations.bg-BG: Мога ли да оставя багажа тук?

mnemonic.title: Maleta, maletero
mnemonic.text: A «maleta» is a suitcase; the car boot, where it rides, is the «maletero».

grammar.title: Puedo + infinitive
grammar.text: «Puedo» (I can) takes a plain infinitive with nothing in between: «puedo dejar», «puedo pagar».

pronunciation.title: Stress on the end: a-QUÍ
pronunciation.text: The accent puts the stress at the end of «aquí»: ah-KEE. The qu is a plain k.

phrases.target: ¿A qué hora hay que dejar la habitación?

translations.en-GB: What time do I have to check out?
translations.bg-BG: До колко часа трябва да освободя стаята?

mnemonic.title: Habitación and inhabit
mnemonic.text: «Habitación» shares a root with “inhabit”: the room you live in. «Dejar la habitación» is to check out.

grammar.title: Impersonal «hay que»
grammar.text: «Hay que» + infinitive means “one has to”, with no person named: «hay que dejar la habitación a las doce».

pronunciation.title: Three silent h's
pronunciation.ipa: [a ˈke ˈo.ɾa ˈaj ke ðeˈxaɾ la a.βi.taˈθjon]
pronunciation.respelling: ah KEH OH-rah EYE keh deh-HAR lah ah-bee-tah-THYON
pronunciation.text: Every h here is silent: «hora» is “OH-rah”, «hay» is “eye” and «habitación» starts “ah-”.

translations.en-GB: Do you have this shirt in another size?
translations.bg-BG: Имате ли тази риза в друг размер?
translations.ru-RU: У вас есть эта рубашка другого размера?

mnemonic.title: Talla: a taller size
mnemonic.text: «Talla» (size) looks like “tall”: picture asking for a taller shirt. «Camisa» is a shirt, like the French “chemise”.

grammar.title: Este or esta
grammar.text: “This” agrees with the noun: «esta camisa» (feminine), «este jersey» (masculine).

pronunciation.title: ll sounds like y
pronunciation.respelling: TYEH-neh ES-tah kah-MEE-sah en OH-trah TAH-yah
pronunciation.text: In Spain «ll» sounds like the y in “yes”: «talla» is “TAH-yah”.

mnemonic.title: Probar, to probe
mnemonic.text: Think of “probe”: «probar» is to test something out, whether a shirt on your back or a tapa on your plate.

grammar.title: Probarse, try on
grammar.text: «Probar» is to try; «probarse» is to try on yourself, so «me» comes along. «Lo» is the garment; say «me la…» for «la camisa».

pronunciation.title: Soft b in probar
pronunciation.text: The b of «probar» sits between vowels, so it's soft: the lips come close but don't touch.

mnemonic.title: Probar → probador
mnemonic.text: A «probador» is where you «probar» (try on). The ending «-dor» can name a place, as in «comedor», dining room.

grammar.title: Está or están
grammar.text: Where something is takes «estar». «Probadores» is plural, so «están»; for one, «¿Dónde está el probador?».

pronunciation.title: Soft d in probadores
pronunciation.text: The d of «probadores» sits between vowels, so it's close to the th in “this”.

translations.en-GB: It's a bit big on me

mnemonic.title: Queda bien, queda grande
mnemonic.text: Picture the fitting-room mirror: «me queda bien» (it fits), «me queda grande» (too big), «me queda pequeño» (too small).

grammar.title: The clothes are the subject
grammar.text: «Quedar» works like «gustar»: the garment is the subject and «me» is the wearer. Plural: «me quedan grandes».

pronunciation.title: n becomes m
pronunciation.text: Before p, the n of «un» turns into m: «un poco» sounds like “oom POH-koh”.

translations.bg-BG: Мога ли да платя с карта?

mnemonic.title: Card on target
mnemonic.text: «Tarjeta» (card) sounds like “target”: picture your card hitting the target as you tap the reader.

grammar.title: Con tarjeta, en efectivo
grammar.text: You pay «con tarjeta» (by card) but «en efectivo» (in cash). No article: never «con una tarjeta» here.

pronunciation.title: The j in tarjeta
pronunciation.text: The j of «tarjeta» is a rasping h, like the ch in Scottish “loch”.

mnemonic.title: Mirar and mirror
mnemonic.text: «Mirar» (to look) sounds like “mirror”, the thing you look into.

grammar.title: Estar + -ando
grammar.text: «Estar» + a verb in «-ando» or «-iendo» says what you're doing right now: «estoy mirando», I'm looking.

pronunciation.title: Gracias with a th
pronunciation.text: In Spain «gracias» has the th of “think”: “GRAH-thyahs”, not “GRAH-see-as”.

mnemonic.title: Of where are you?
mnemonic.text: «¿De dónde eres?» is word for word “Of where are you?”: picture someone made of their home town.

grammar.title: Ser for origin
grammar.text: «Eres» is the tú form of ser, the verb for where you come from. Answer «Soy de…»: the «de» comes first, never at the end.

pronunciation.title: Soft d in dónde
pronunciation.text: After de, the d of dónde goes soft, close to the th in “this”. The d after n stays hard.

mnemonic.title: Gusto, as in English
mnemonic.text: English “with gusto” shares its Latin root: «gusto» is pleasure or taste. «Mucho gusto» is literally “much pleasure”.

grammar.title: «Mucho» agrees
grammar.text: «Mucho» matches its noun. «Gusto» is masculine, so «mucho»; with a feminine noun it's «mucha»: «mucha suerte» (good luck).

pronunciation.title: A soft g
pronunciation.text: After a vowel, the g of gusto softens: the back of the tongue nears the palate but doesn't close.

translations.en-GB: How long have you been here?

mnemonic.title: You carry the time
mnemonic.text: «Llevar» means “to carry”: literally “how much time do you carry here?”. Picture the weeks piled up in your arms.

grammar.title: Present, not “have been”
grammar.text: Spanish uses the present «llevas» where English says “have you been”. Answer the same way: «Llevo dos semanas» (I've been here two weeks).

pronunciation.title: The ll in llevas
pronunciation.text: In most of Spain ll sounds like the y in “yes”: YEH-vahs.

mnemonic.title: An apprentice learns
mnemonic.text: «Aprender» (to learn) shares its Latin root with “apprentice”, someone who is learning a trade.

grammar.title: Estar + -ndo
grammar.text: «Estoy aprendiendo» is estar plus the -ndo form, like English “-ing”: aprender → aprendiendo, hablar → hablando.

pronunciation.title: A tapped r
pronunciation.text: The r in aprendiendo is one quick tap, like the tt in American “butter”.

mnemonic.title: Leave some space
mnemonic.text: «Despacio» (slowly) comes from «de espacio», “with space”: picture space between each word.

grammar.title: Poder + infinitive
grammar.text: «Puedes» is poder with o → ue. The next verb stays in the infinitive, with no “to”: «¿Puedes repetir?» (Can you repeat?).

pronunciation.title: The c in despacio
pronunciation.text: In Spain the c of despacio sounds like the th in “think”: des-PAH-thyoh.

mnemonic.title: Inglés and Inglaterra
mnemonic.text: «Inglés» (English) pairs with «Inglaterra» (England), as «español» pairs with «España».

grammar.title: No “do” needed
grammar.text: Spanish has no “do” for questions: «Hablas inglés» (you speak English) becomes a question just by rising at the end.

pronunciation.title: Silent h
pronunciation.text: The h of hablas is silent: start straight on the a.

mnemonic.title: Calor and calorie
mnemonic.text: «Calor» (heat) is the Latin root of “calorie”, a unit of heat.

grammar.title: Weather with hacer
grammar.text: Spanish uses «hacer» for much of the weather: «hace calor», «hace frío», «hace sol». «¡Qué…!» turns it into an exclamation.

pronunciation.title: The c in hace
pronunciation.text: In Spain the c of hace sounds like the th in “think”: AH-theh.

mnemonic.title: Frío and frigid
mnemonic.text: «Frío» (cold) comes from the same Latin word as “frigid”; “refrigerator” is a cousin.

grammar.title: Mucho, not muy
grammar.text: «Frío» is a noun here (the cold), so it takes «mucho», not «muy». Of a thing, it's an adjective: «el café está muy frío».

pronunciation.title: Two syllables in frío
pronunciation.text: Frío has two syllables, FREE-oh: the accent on í keeps the i and o apart.

translations.en-GB: Is it going to rain tomorrow?

mnemonic.title: Two mañanas
mnemonic.text: «Mañana» is “tomorrow”; «la mañana» is “the morning”. So «mañana por la mañana» is tomorrow morning.

grammar.title: Ir a + infinitive
grammar.text: «Va a llover» is ir a + infinitive, the everyday way to say what's going to happen: «voy a salir» (I'm going to go out).

pronunciation.title: The v in va
pronunciation.text: Spanish v is a b sound: a full b at the start of va, a soft one inside llover.

mnemonic.title: Family of nube
mnemonic.text: «Nublado» is family with «nube» (cloud): the sky has clouded over. Nube, nublarse, nublado.

grammar.title: Está for the sky now
grammar.text: What the sky looks like now takes «está»: «está nublado», «está lloviendo». Heat and cold take «hace».

pronunciation.title: The soft -ado
pronunciation.text: The d in -ado is soft, like the th in “this”; in relaxed speech in Spain it almost disappears.

translations.en-GB: It's nice weather for a walk

mnemonic.title: Pasear and the paseo
mnemonic.text: «Pasear» is to stroll, and a stroll is «un paseo». A «paseo» is also a promenade, like Madrid's Paseo del Prado.

grammar.title: Bueno becomes buen
grammar.text: «Bueno» drops its -o before a masculine singular noun: «buen tiempo», «buen día». After the noun it stays: «el tiempo es bueno».

pronunciation.title: Three syllables in pasear
pronunciation.text: Pasear has three syllables, pa-se-AR: keep the e and the a apart.

mnemonic.title: It stops the water
mnemonic.text: «Paraguas» joins «para» (from parar, to stop) and «aguas» (waters). A «parasol» stops the sun the same way.

grammar.title: Te on the end
grammar.text: In a tú command the pronoun joins the end: «lleva» + «te» → «llévate». The written accent keeps the stress where it was.

pronunciation.title: The gwa in paraguas
pronunciation.text: Gua sounds like “gwa”, with a soft g: the back of the tongue doesn't quite close.

mnemonic.title: A plan that stays put
mnemonic.text: «Quedar» is to remain, and also to arrange to meet: a plan you make is one that stays put. «¿Quedamos mañana?», shall we meet tomorrow?

grammar.title: Present as “shall we”
grammar.text: Spanish uses the present «quedamos» to suggest a plan, like English “shall we…?”. The -amos ending means “we”.

pronunciation.title: Qu is just k
pronunciation.text: Qu is a plain k sound, with no w after it: keh-DAH-mos.

translations.bg-BG: Удобно ли ти е в седем?

mnemonic.title: Does it come well?
mnemonic.text: Literally “does it come well to you at seven?”. A time that doesn't suit «viene mal»: it comes badly.

grammar.title: «A las» for times
grammar.text: Clock times take «a las» (at the): «a las siete». One o'clock is singular: «a la una».

pronunciation.title: V and b alike
pronunciation.respelling: teh BYEH-neh BYEN ah lahs SYEH-teh
pronunciation.text: V and b sound the same in Spanish: viene and bien both start with a soft b.

mnemonic.title: Plaza, place, piazza
mnemonic.text: «Plaza» shares its Latin root with “place” and Italian “piazza”. A town's main square is often «la Plaza Mayor».

grammar.title: Nos: each other
grammar.text: «Nos vemos» is literally “we see each other”: «nos» makes the action mutual. On its own, «¡Nos vemos!» means “see you!”.

pronunciation.title: The z in plaza
pronunciation.text: In Spain the z of plaza sounds like the th in “think”: PLAH-thah.

phrases.target: Llego un poco tarde, lo siento

translations.en-GB: I'm running a bit late, sorry

mnemonic.title: Tarde and tardy
mnemonic.text: «Tarde» (late) shares its Latin root with English “tardy”. As a noun, «la tarde» is the afternoon.

grammar.title: Present for a delay
grammar.text: Spanish uses the present «llego» (I arrive) for a delay happening now: «Llego tarde» is “I'm running late”.

pronunciation.title: Soft g in llego
pronunciation.respelling: YEH-goh oom POH-koh TAR-deh, loh SYEN-toh
pronunciation.text: Between vowels the g of llego is soft: the back of the tongue nears the palate without closing.

translations.en-GB: What do you feel like doing?

mnemonic.title: Apetece and appetite
mnemonic.text: «Apetecer» (to fancy) shares its Latin root with “appetite”: what do you have an appetite to do?

grammar.title: Works like gustar
grammar.text: «Apetecer» works like «gustar»: the thing is the subject and «te» is who fancies it. «Me apetece un café» (I fancy a coffee).

pronunciation.title: Two th sounds
pronunciation.text: In Spain the c of apetece and of hacer is the th in “think”; the h is silent.

translations.ru-RU: Сегодня не могу, может, в другой день?

mnemonic.title: Otro sounds like other
mnemonic.text: «Otro» sounds like “other” and means it: «otro día» is another day.

grammar.title: No goes first
grammar.text: «No» goes straight before the verb: «no puedo» (I can't). «Puedo» is poder with o → ue.

pronunciation.title: Soft d in día
pronunciation.text: After otro, the d of día is soft, like the th in “this”.

translations.en-GB: Where do I check in my luggage?

mnemonic.title: «Facturar», “to invoice”
mnemonic.text: «Facturar» also means “to invoice”: you hand over your case and get a receipt. «Equipaje» shares its root with English “equip”.

grammar.title: Impersonal «se»
grammar.text: «Se» + verb makes it impersonal: “where is it checked in?”. The verb agrees with the thing: «¿Dónde se facturan las maletas?».

pronunciation.title: The throaty j
pronunciation.text: The j in «equipaje» is a throaty sound, like the ch in Scottish “loch”.

phrases.target: Mi vuelo sale a las diez

mnemonic.title: «Sale» is not a sale
mnemonic.text: «Sale» is from «salir», “to leave”, like «salida»: the exit, and the departures board at the airport.

grammar.title: «A las» for times
grammar.text: Clock times take «a las» + the hour: «a las diez». One o'clock is singular: «a la una».

pronunciation.title: Castilian z
pronunciation.respelling: mee VWEH-loh SAH-leh ah lahs DYETH
pronunciation.text: In Spain the z in «diez» sounds like the th in “think”.

mnemonic.title: A boat in «embarque»
mnemonic.text: «Embarque» holds «barca», “boat”, just like English “embark”. Boarding a plane kept the old ship word.

grammar.title: «Cuál» before «es»
grammar.text: Before «es», ask «¿cuál?», not «¿qué?»: «¿Cuál es la puerta?». «¿Qué es?» asks for a definition.

pronunciation.title: The «ue» glide
pronunciation.respelling: KWAL es lah PWER-tah deh em-BAR-keh
pronunciation.text: The «ue» in «puerta» glides into one syllable: “pweh”.

mnemonic.title: Maleta, maletero
mnemonic.text: A «maleta» is a suitcase; the car boot you put it in is the «maletero».

grammar.title: «He» + participle
grammar.text: «He perdido» is «haber» + participle, like English “I have lost”. Spain uses it for things that have just happened.

pronunciation.title: A silent h
pronunciation.text: The h of «he» is silent: say just “eh”.

mnemonic.title: Running behind
mnemonic.text: «Retraso» contains «tras», “behind”, as in «atrás»: the flight is running behind.

grammar.title: «Ir con retraso»
grammar.text: Spanish says the flight “goes with delay”: «va con retraso», from «ir». It works for trains and buses too.

pronunciation.title: A rolled r
pronunciation.text: The r at the start of «retraso» is rolled, like rr; the r after t is a single tap.

translations.en-GB: Can I take this as hand luggage?
translations.bg-BG: Мога ли да взема това като ръчен багаж?
translations.ru-RU: Можно взять это в ручную кладь?

mnemonic.title: Like «para llevar»
mnemonic.text: «Llevar» is “to take with you”, the same verb as «para llevar», a takeaway coffee. «En cabina» is “in the cabin”.

grammar.title: «Poder» + infinitive
grammar.text: «Puedo» is «poder» with o → ue, and the next verb stays in the infinitive: «puedo llevar», with nothing in between.

pronunciation.title: The ll sound
pronunciation.text: In Spain «ll» sounds close to the y in “yes”.

mnemonic.title: Think of “aid”
mnemonic.text: Think of English “aid”: «ayuda» and “aid” come from the same Latin verb.

grammar.title: Adding «me»
grammar.text: «¡Ayuda!» works as a shout, like “Help!”. To ask someone directly, add «me»: «¡Ayúdeme!» (usted), «¡Ayúdame!» (tú).

pronunciation.title: A soft d
pronunciation.text: The d between vowels is soft, close to the th in “this”.

phrases.target: Llame a una ambulancia, por favor

mnemonic.title: «Llamar» and «me llamo»
mnemonic.text: «Llamar» means “to call”, the same verb as «me llamo…», “I'm called…”.

grammar.title: Polite command
grammar.text: «Llame» is the usted command of «llamar»: -ar verbs switch their a to e. To a friend: «Llama a una ambulancia».

pronunciation.title: Castilian c
pronunciation.respelling: YAH-meh ah OO-nah am-boo-LAN-thyah, por fah-VOR
pronunciation.text: The c before i in «ambulancia» sounds like the th in “think”.

mnemonic.title: Robar is “rob”
mnemonic.text: «Robar» is English “rob”: «me han robado», “they've robbed me”. A «cartera» is a wallet.

grammar.title: An unnamed “they”
grammar.text: Spanish leaves the thief unnamed and uses “they”: «me han robado», “they've robbed me”. «Me» is the person robbed.

pronunciation.title: Rolled r, tapped r
pronunciation.text: The r of «robado» is rolled; the r's in «cartera» are single quick taps.

mnemonic.title: The commissioner's office
mnemonic.text: A «comisaría» is where the «comisario», the police commissioner, works.

grammar.title: «Estar» for places
grammar.text: Where something is takes «estar»: «¿Dónde está…?». «Ser» says what something is.

pronunciation.title: Two syllables in «ía»
pronunciation.text: The accent on «í» splits «ía» into two syllables: ri-a, with the stress on ri.

mnemonic.title: Lost in perdition
mnemonic.text: «Perdido» (lost) sounds like “perdition”: picture yourself so lost it feels like the end of the world. «Me he perdido», I’m lost.

grammar.title: Reflexive «perderse»
grammar.text: «Perderse» is “to get lost”, and «me» goes before «he». The same pattern: «te has perdido», «nos hemos perdido».

pronunciation.title: Soft d's
pronunciation.text: Both d's in «perdido» are soft, close to the th in “this”.

mnemonic.title: Alguien, algo, nadie
mnemonic.text: «Alguien» is “someone”, in the family of «algo» (something) and «alguno» (some). Its opposite is «nadie».

grammar.title: Questions by tone
grammar.text: A yes/no question keeps the word order of a statement: only the rising tone and «¿…?» mark it.

pronunciation.title: A silent u
pronunciation.text: The u in «alguien» is silent; it only keeps the g hard: AL-gyen.

phrases.target: Tengo una reunión a las diez

translations.en-GB: I have a meeting at ten

mnemonic.title: Not just a reunion
mnemonic.text: In Spanish a «reunión» is any meeting, from a quick team call to a board meeting, not just a “reunion” of old friends.

grammar.title: Tener → tengo
grammar.text: «Tener» adds a g in the “I” form: «tengo», but «tienes» and «tiene» for “you” and “he” or “she”.

pronunciation.title: ng in «tengo»
pronunciation.respelling: TENG-goh OO-nah rreh-oo-NYON ah lahs DYETH
pronunciation.text: The n in «tengo» sounds like the ng in “finger”.

translations.en-GB: Can you send me the report?
translations.bg-BG: Може ли да ми пратиш доклада?

mnemonic.title: Mandar: send and command
mnemonic.text: «Mandar» means both “to send” and “to order”: English “mandate” shares the root. An «informe» is what informs you: a report.

grammar.title: Where «me» goes
grammar.text: «Me» can go before «puedes» or on the end: «¿Puedes mandarme el informe?» means the same.

pronunciation.title: Soft d, hard d
pronunciation.text: The d in «puedes» is soft, like the th in “this”; after n, in «mandar», it is a hard d.

translations.en-GB: I work from home on Fridays
translations.ru-RU: По пятницам я работаю из дома

mnemonic.title: Venus's day
mnemonic.text: «Viernes» is Venus's day, from Latin; «martes» is Mars's day and «lunes» the Moon's.

grammar.title: «Los viernes» for habits
grammar.text: «Los viernes» means “on Fridays”, every week; «el viernes» is one Friday. Spanish needs no word for “on”.

pronunciation.title: The throaty j
pronunciation.text: The j in «trabajo» is throaty, like the ch in Scottish “loch”.

mnemonic.title: «Un momentito»
mnemonic.text: «Momento» is English “moment”. The diminutive makes it lighter: «¿Tienes un momentito?».

grammar.title: Tú or usted
grammar.text: «Tienes» is the tú form, fine with colleagues in Spain. To a stranger or an important client: «¿Tiene un momento?».

pronunciation.title: n turns to m
pronunciation.text: Before the m of «momento», the n of «un» becomes m: “oom-moh-MEN-toh”.

mnemonic.title: The end of the line
mnemonic.text: «Terminar» is “to finish”: think of a “terminal”, the end of the line.

grammar.title: Present for a promise
grammar.text: The present tense can promise the near future: «lo termino hoy», “I'll finish it today”. «Lo» (it) goes before the verb.

pronunciation.title: Stress on «mi»
pronunciation.text: Stress «mi»: «termino» is “I finish”, but «terminó» means “it finished”.

translations.en-GB: What time do you finish work?

mnemonic.title: Hora, hour
mnemonic.text: «Hora» is English “hour”, and just as in “hour”, the h is silent.

grammar.title: De + el = del
grammar.text: «De» + «el» always merge into «del»: «sales del trabajo». Likewise «a» + «el» → «al».

pronunciation.title: A tapped r
pronunciation.respelling: ah KEH OH-rah SAH-les del trah-BAH-hoh
pronunciation.text: The r in «hora» is one quick tap, like the tt in American “butter”.

mnemonic.title: A countersign
mnemonic.text: «Contraseña» is «contra» + «seña» (“sign”), like the English “countersign”: the word you give back to be let in.

grammar.title: «¿Cuál es…?» for specifics
grammar.text: To ask for a specific piece of information, use «¿Cuál es…?». «¿Qué es la contraseña?» would ask what a password is.

pronunciation.title: The ñ in contraseña
pronunciation.respelling: KWAL es lah kon-trah-SEH-nyah del WEE-fee
pronunciation.text: ñ sounds like the ny in “canyon”: con-tra-SE-ña.

mnemonic.title: The sin of a flat battery
mnemonic.text: «Sin» (without) sounds like “sin”: picture the sin of leaving home without charging your phone. «Sin batería», without battery.

grammar.title: Just happened: the perfect
grammar.text: In Spain, something that has just happened goes in the perfect: «he» + participle, as in «me he quedado». «Me» comes before «he».

pronunciation.title: Soft d in quedado
pronunciation.text: Both d's in «quedado» are soft, close to the th in “this”.

translations.en-GB: Can I charge my phone here?
translations.bg-BG: Мога ли да си заредя телефона тук?

mnemonic.title: Loading cargo
mnemonic.text: «Cargar» (to charge) looks like “cargo”: it also means to load, so picture loading your phone with power like cargo onto a ship.

grammar.title: o becomes ue
grammar.text: When stressed, the o of «poder» becomes ue: «puedo», «puedes», but «podemos». The verb after it stays in the infinitive: «cargar».

pronunciation.title: A soft v in móvil
pronunciation.text: The v of «móvil» is a soft b: the lips come close but don't touch.

mnemonic.title: Same verb as «me llamo»
mnemonic.text: It's the verb of «me llamo…» (“my name is…”, literally “I call myself”). «Te llamo» is “I call you”.

grammar.title: Present for a plan
grammar.text: Spanish often uses the present for a near plan: «te llamo luego», “I'll call you later”. «Te» goes before the verb.

pronunciation.title: ll sounds like y
pronunciation.text: In Spain «ll» sounds like the y in “yes”: YAH-moh.

mnemonic.title: Coverage, from «cubrir»
mnemonic.text: «Cobertura» is “coverage”, a relative of «cubrir» (“to cover”): no coverage, no signal.

grammar.title: Just «no» before the verb
grammar.text: Spanish needs no “don't”: put «no» right before the verb. «Tengo» (I have) → «no tengo» (I haven't got).

pronunciation.title: ng in tengo
pronunciation.text: Before g, the n of «tengo» sounds like the ng in “finger”.

translations.bg-BG: Ще ми дадеш ли номера си?

mnemonic.title: «Dar», as in “data”
mnemonic.text: «Das» is from «dar», “to give”. English “data”, literally “things given”, comes from the same Latin verb.

grammar.title: Tu or tú
grammar.text: «Tu» without an accent is “your”; «tú» with one is “you”: «tú tienes tu número».

pronunciation.title: NU-me-ro
pronunciation.text: Stress the first syllable of «número», as the accent shows.

mnemonic.title: Her, your sister
mnemonic.text: «Hermana» (sister) starts with “her”: picture her, your sister, waving at you. A brother is «hermano».

grammar.title: Un hermano, una hermana
grammar.text: “A” agrees with the noun: «un» for masculine, «una» for feminine. Most nouns in -o are masculine and most in -a feminine.

pronunciation.title: A silent h
pronunciation.text: The h of «hermana» is silent: er-MAH-nah.

mnemonic.title: Hijo, as in «hidalgo»
mnemonic.text: «Hijo» (son) hides in «hidalgo», a nobleman: from «hijo de algo», “son of something”.

grammar.title: Hijos: sons and daughters
grammar.text: A masculine plural covers a mixed group: «hijos» is children of either sex, as «padres» is “parents”.

pronunciation.title: The j in hijos
pronunciation.text: The j is a rasping h, like the ch in Scottish “loch”. The h at the start is silent.

phrases.target: Mis padres viven en el campo

translations.en-GB: My parents live in the countryside

mnemonic.title: Campo, as in “campus”
mnemonic.text: «Campo» shares its Latin root with “campus” and “camp”: a field. «El campo» is the countryside.

grammar.title: Mi, mis
grammar.text: «Mi» (my) becomes «mis» before a plural: «mi padre», «mis padres». It doesn't change for masculine or feminine.

pronunciation.title: V sounds like b
pronunciation.respelling: mees PAH-dres VEE-ven en el KAHM-poh
pronunciation.text: Spanish b and v sound the same: both v's in «viven» are a soft b, the lips almost touching.

translations.bg-BG: Синът ми е на пет години

mnemonic.title: Año, as in “annual”
mnemonic.text: The ñ of «año» was once a double n, as in Latin annus; English keeps it in “annual” and “anniversary”.

grammar.title: Age uses «tener»
grammar.text: Spanish has years rather than being them: «tiene cinco años», literally “has five years”.

pronunciation.title: Castilian th in cinco
pronunciation.text: In Spain the first c of «cinco» sounds like the th in “think”; the second is a plain k.

phrases.target: Este fin de semana vamos a ver a mis abuelos

translations.en-GB: This weekend we're visiting my grandparents
translations.bg-BG: Този уикенд ще ходим при баба и дядо
translations.ru-RU: В эти выходные мы едем к бабушке с дедушкой

mnemonic.title: End of week, «el finde»
mnemonic.text: «Fin de semana» is word for word “end of week”. In Spain friends shorten it to «el finde».

grammar.title: The personal «a»
grammar.text: When the object of a verb is a person, Spanish puts «a» before it: «ver a mis abuelos», but «ver la tele».

pronunciation.title: BWE in abuelos
pronunciation.ipa: [ˈes.te ˈfin de seˈma.na ˈβa.mos a ˈβeɾ a mis aˈβwe.los]
pronunciation.respelling: ES-teh feen deh seh-MAH-nah VAH-mos ah VER ah mees ah-BWEH-los
pronunciation.text: «Bue» in «abuelos» is one syllable, “bweh”, with a soft b.

mnemonic.title: -y becomes «-ia»
mnemonic.text: English words in -y often end in «-ia» in Spanish: family → «familia», pharmacy → «farmacia», history → «historia».

grammar.title: «Estar» for how things are
grammar.text: Ask how someone is with «estar»: «¿Cómo está…?». With «ser», «¿Cómo es…?» asks what they're like.

pronunciation.title: fa-MI-lia
pronunciation.text: The «lia» at the end of «familia» is one syllable, “lyah”.

phrases.target: Quería reservar una mesa para cuatro

translations.en-GB: I'd like to book a table for four
translations.bg-BG: Искам да запазя маса за четирима

mnemonic.title: Mesa, like the flat hill
mnemonic.text: A «mesa» is a table. English borrowed the word for a flat-topped hill that looks like one.

grammar.title: Polite «quería»
grammar.text: «Quería» (“I wanted”) is the polite way to ask for something in Spain, softer than «quiero» (“I want”).

pronunciation.title: Rolled r in reservar
pronunciation.respelling: keh-REE-ah reh-ser-VAR OO-nah MEH-sah PAH-rah KWAH-troh
pronunciation.text: The r at the start of «reservar» is rolled; every other r here is a single tap.

translations.en-GB: Do you have a table for tonight?
translations.bg-BG: Имате ли свободна маса за довечера?
translations.ru-RU: У вас есть столик на сегодня вечером?

mnemonic.title: Noche, as in “nocturnal”
mnemonic.text: «Esta noche» is “tonight”, literally “this night”. «Noche» shares its Latin root with “nocturnal”.

grammar.title: No «una» needed
grammar.text: Asking whether something is available, Spanish often drops «una»: «¿Tienen mesa?», «¿Tienes coche?».

pronunciation.title: Ch as in “church”
pronunciation.text: The ch of «noche» is the ch in “church”, and the final e is short and clear.

mnemonic.title: Nombre, like “nominate”
mnemonic.text: «Nombre» comes from Latin nomen, the root of “noun” and “nominate”. «A nombre de» is “in the name of”.

grammar.title: Prepositions come first
grammar.text: Spanish never ends a question on a preposition: “whose name is it under?” becomes «¿A nombre de quién?», “in the name of whom?”.

pronunciation.title: Silent u in quién
pronunciation.text: In «quién» the u is silent: it's one syllable, “kyen”.

mnemonic.title: Hay sounds like “eye”
mnemonic.text: «Hay» sounds like the English “eye” and means “there is” or “there are”. «Hay que…» is “one has to…”.

grammar.title: «Hay que» + infinitive
grammar.text: «Hay que» + infinitive means “you have to” in general, naming nobody: «hay que reservar», “booking is needed”.

pronunciation.title: Soft v in reservar
pronunciation.text: After r, the v of «reservar» is a soft b: the lips come close but don't touch.

translations.en-GB: There are two of us, at nine

mnemonic.title: Nueve, not nuevo
mnemonic.text: «Nueve» (nine) and «nuevo» (new) differ only in the last letter. Picture a new clock striking nine.

grammar.title: «A las» for the time
grammar.text: Clock times take «las», since «horas» (hours) is feminine plural: «a las nueve», but «a la una» for one o'clock.

pronunciation.title: NWE-ve
pronunciation.text: «Nue» is one syllable, “nweh”, and the v is a soft b.

translations.en-GB: We have to cancel the booking

mnemonic.title: Two easy cognates
mnemonic.text: «Cancelar» is “cancel” and «reserva» is “reservation”. In Spain a booking is «una reserva»; «reservación» is Latin American.

grammar.title: «Tener que» + infinitive
grammar.text: «Tener que» + infinitive is “to have to”, for a named person: «tenemos que cancelar». «Hay que» says it in general.

pronunciation.title: Th in cancelar
pronunciation.text: In Spain the c before e in «cancelar» sounds like the th in “think”.

translations.en-GB: Where is there a pharmacy nearby?

mnemonic.title: Аптека, apothecary
mnemonic.text: «Аптека» shares its Greek root with “apothecary”, an old English word for a chemist.

grammar.title: «Има», there is
grammar.text: «Има» means “there is” or “there are”: «има аптека», «има аптеки». «Къде има…?» asks for any one nearby.

pronunciation.title: The ъ in къде
pronunciation.text: «Ъ» in «къде» is short and neutral, like the a in “about”.

translations.en-GB: Do you have something for a headache?
translations.ru-RU: У вас есть что-нибудь от головной боли?

mnemonic.title: Head + pain
mnemonic.text: «Главоболие» joins «глава» (head) and «бол-», as in «болка» (pain): a head-pain, just like “headache”.

grammar.title: Medicine «против»
grammar.text: «Против» (against) names what a remedy fights: «нещо против главоболие», something for a headache.

pronunciation.title: gla-vo-BO-li-e
pronunciation.text: Stress «главоболие» on «бо»: gla-vo-BO-lee-e, and say the final «-ие» in full.

mnemonic.title: Gurgle for гърло
mnemonic.text: «Гърло» (throat) starts like “gurgle”; with “the” it becomes «гърлото».

grammar.title: «Ме» follows the verb
grammar.text: The throat is the subject: «боли ме гърлото», “the throat hurts me”. «Ме» can't start a sentence, so it comes after «боли».

pronunciation.title: Stressed ъ
pronunciation.text: Stressed «ъ» sounds like the u in “fur”: GUR-lo-to.

translations.en-GB: I need to go to the doctor

mnemonic.title: Лекар and лекарство
mnemonic.text: «Лекар» (doctor) and «лекарство» (medicine) share the root «лек», a cure.

grammar.title: No infinitive
grammar.text: Bulgarian has no infinitive: «трябва да» takes a verb with a person ending, «трябва да отида», I have to go.

pronunciation.title: The ря in трябва
pronunciation.text: «Ря» in «трябва» is r with a quick y after it: TRYAB-va.

mnemonic.title: Words you already know
mnemonic.text: «Алергия» and «пеницилин» are “allergy” and “penicillin” in Cyrillic: sound them out letter by letter and you already know them.

grammar.title: Allergic «към»
grammar.text: An allergy is «към» (towards) its cause: «алергия към пеницилин», «алергия към ядки».

pronunciation.title: ц is ts
pronunciation.text: «Ц» sounds like the ts in “cats”: pe-nee-tsee-LEEN.

phrases.target: Имам резервация на името на Петров

translations.en-GB: I have a booking under the name Petrov
translations.ru-RU: У меня бронь на имя Петров

mnemonic.title: -ция is -tion
mnemonic.text: «Резервация» is “reservation” in Cyrillic: the ending «-ция» matches English “-tion”, as in «информация».

grammar.title: «На» means “of”
grammar.text: With no case endings, Bulgarian uses «на» for “of”: «името на Петров», Petrov's name. «Име» + «-то» is “the name”.

pronunciation.title: Final в sounds like f
pronunciation.respelling: EE-mam re-zer-VA-tsee-ya na EE-me-to na PET-rof
pronunciation.text: At the end of a word «в» sounds like f: «Петров» is “PET-rof”.

mnemonic.title: Not a Russian snack
mnemonic.text: «Закуска» is breakfast in Bulgarian; in Russian the same word means a starter or snack.

grammar.title: The counting form
grammar.text: After «колко» and numbers, «час» takes the counting form «часа»: «в колко часа», «в осем часа».

pronunciation.title: В before к is f
pronunciation.text: «В» before «колко» is a quick f, joined to the next word: “f KOL-ko”.

mnemonic.title: A carpet for a towel
mnemonic.text: «Кърпа» (KUR-pa) sounds like the start of “carpet”: picture drying yourself with a small carpet.

grammar.title: «Може ли» + a thing
grammar.text: «Може ли…?» plus just a noun is a polite request, no verb needed: «може ли още една кърпа?», «може ли сметката?».

pronunciation.title: щ is sht
pronunciation.text: «Щ» is always sh + t: «още» sounds like “OSH-te”.

mnemonic.title: Климатик, climate
mnemonic.text: «Климатик» is built on «климат», climate: it's the machine that sets a room's climate.

grammar.title: Full article «-ът»
grammar.text: A masculine subject takes the full article «-ът»: «климатикът не работи». As an object it's «-а»: «оправете климатика».

pronunciation.title: The -ът ending
pronunciation.text: The ending «-ът» is unstressed and short, like the a in “about”: klee-ma-TEE-kut.

phrases.target: Мога ли да оставя багажа си тук?

translations.en-GB: Can I leave my luggage here?

mnemonic.title: Багаж, baggage
mnemonic.text: «Багаж» sounds like “baggage” and, like it, covers all your bags at once.

grammar.title: Reflexive «си»
grammar.text: «Си» means “one's own”, pointing back to whoever acts: «багажа си», my luggage. It follows the noun with its article.

pronunciation.title: The вя in оставя
pronunciation.ipa: [ˈmɔɡɐ li dɐ osˈtavʲɐ bɐˈɡaʒɐ si ˈtuk]
pronunciation.respelling: MO-ga lee da os-TA-vya ba-GA-zha see TOOK
pronunciation.text: «Вя» is v with a quick y after it: os-TA-vya.

phrases.target: Имате ли това в по-голям размер?

translations.en-GB: Do you have this in a bigger size?
translations.ru-RU: У вас есть это на размер больше?

mnemonic.title: Goliath is голям
mnemonic.text: «Голям» (big) starts like “Goliath”, the giant. Its opposite is «малък», small.

grammar.title: «По-» for bigger
grammar.text: Put «по-» before any adjective for “more”: «голям» (big) → «по-голям» (bigger), «малък» → «по-малък».

pronunciation.title: Two stresses: PO-go-LYAM
pronunciation.ipa: [ˈimɐtɛ li toˈva f ˈpɔ ɡoˈʎam rɐzˈmɛr]
pronunciation.respelling: EE-ma-te lee to-VA f PO-go-LYAM raz-MER
pronunciation.text: «По-» carries its own stress, so «по-голям» has two: PO-go-LYAM.

mnemonic.title: Пробвам, пробна
mnemonic.text: «Пробвам» (to try) sounds like “probe”; the room where you try things on is the «пробна».

grammar.title: «Го» before the verb
grammar.text: «Го» (it) sits right before the verb, after «да»: «да го пробвам». For a feminine garment use «я»: «да я пробвам».

pronunciation.title: Say the б and the в
pronunciation.text: Say both consonants in «пробвам»: PROB-vam, with a clear b before the v.

mnemonic.title: From пробвам
mnemonic.text: A «пробна» is the room where you «пробвам» (try on). More than one, with “the”: «пробните».

grammar.title: Plural “the” is «-те»
grammar.text: Plurals ending in «-и» take «-те» for “the”: «пробни» → «пробните». «Са» means “are”.

pronunciation.title: PROB-ni-te
pronunciation.text: Stress the first syllable of «пробните» and keep the b clear before the n: PROB-nee-te.

mnemonic.title: Раз- + гледам
mnemonic.text: «Гледам» is to look; «раз-» spreads it around, so «разглеждам» is looking about: browsing.

grammar.title: The ending says “I”
grammar.text: The ending «-м» already means “I”, so the pronoun is dropped: «разглеждам», I'm looking.

pronunciation.title: bla-go-da-RYA
pronunciation.text: «Благодаря» is stressed on the last syllable: bla-go-da-RYA.

phrases.target: Мога ли да платя с карта?

mnemonic.title: Paying with a map
mnemonic.text: «Карта» is a bank card and also a map, as in «карта на града», a city map: picture trying to pay with a map.

grammar.title: «Мога» + «да»
grammar.text: «Мога» is “I can”. It takes «да» and a verb with a person ending, never an infinitive: «мога ли да платя», can I pay.

pronunciation.title: The тя in платя
pronunciation.respelling: MO-ga lee da pla-TYA s KAR-ta
pronunciation.text: «Тя» is t with a quick y after it, and it takes the stress: pla-TYA.

mnemonic.title: From + where
mnemonic.text: «Откъде» joins «от» (from) and «къде» (where). «Къде си?» on its own asks where you are right now.

grammar.title: «Си»: you are
grammar.text: «Си» means “you are”, from «съм» (to be). Like «съм», it never starts a sentence: «От Лондон съм» (I'm from London).

pronunciation.title: ot-ka-DE
pronunciation.text: Stress the last syllable, де; the unstressed ъ is a short, neutral “uh”.

mnemonic.title: With what, literally
mnemonic.text: Word for word it's “with what yourself do-you-occupy?”: «с какво» is “with what”, and «се» is “yourself”.

grammar.title: Where «се» goes
grammar.text: «Се» comes before the verb, «С какво се занимаваш?», unless the verb comes first: then it follows, «Занимавам се с музика» (I do music).

pronunciation.title: Какво sounds kak-FO
pronunciation.text: After к, the в of какво sounds like f: kak-FO.

phrases.target: Приятно ми е да се запознаем

mnemonic.title: The root зна-: to know
mnemonic.text: «Запознаем» shares its root with «знам» (I know): meeting someone is getting to know them.

grammar.title: No infinitive: «да»
grammar.text: Bulgarian has no infinitive: “to meet” is «да» + a present form, «да се запознаем», literally “that we get acquainted”.

pronunciation.title: za-poz-NA-em
pronunciation.respelling: pree-YAT-no mee eh da seh za-poz-NA-em
pronunciation.text: Stress на in запознаем, and keep а and е as two syllables: NA-em.

mnemonic.title: Уча, учител, ученик
mnemonic.text: «Уча» (I learn) gives «учител» (teacher) and «ученик» (pupil): one word family.

grammar.title: One present tense
grammar.text: Bulgarian has one present: «уча» is both “I learn” and “I'm learning”. No «аз» (I) is needed; the ending shows who.

pronunciation.title: The ъ in български
pronunciation.text: Stressed ъ is like the u in “but”, said further back in the mouth: BUHL-gar-skee.

mnemonic.title: Бавно or бързо
mnemonic.text: «Бавно» (slowly) and «бързо» (fast) both start with б: learn them as a pair of opposites.

grammar.title: «По-» makes “more”
grammar.text: «По-» with a hyphen makes the comparative: бавно → по-бавно (more slowly), добре → по-добре (better).

pronunciation.title: go-VO-reesh
pronunciation.text: Stress the middle syllable of говориш: go-VO-reesh.

mnemonic.title: Горещо and горя
mnemonic.text: «Горещо» (hot) is family with «горя» (to burn): hot enough to burn.

grammar.title: «Колко» in exclamations
grammar.text: «Колко» (how much) also opens exclamations: «Колко е хубаво!» (How lovely!). The short «е» comes right after it.

pronunciation.title: Щ is sht
pronunciation.text: Щ is “sht”, as in “ashtray”: go-RESH-to.

mnemonic.title: Студ, the cold
mnemonic.text: The noun is «студ» (the cold); «студено» is how it feels. Its opposite is «топло» (warm).

grammar.title: Weather ends in -о
grammar.text: Weather words take the -о ending: студено, топло, горещо. There's no “it”: just «е» (is), after the first word.

pronunciation.title: The mn in много
pronunciation.text: Много starts with m and n together, no vowel between: MNO-go.

translations.en-GB: Is it going to rain tomorrow?

mnemonic.title: Вали: it's falling
mnemonic.text: «Вали» is used for rain and snow alike: «вали сняг» (it's snowing). On its own, «вали» means it's raining.

grammar.title: «Ще» for the future
grammar.text: «Ще» + present makes the future: «вали» (it rains) → «ще вали» (it will rain). «Ли» after the verb makes it a question.

pronunciation.title: Ще is shteh
pronunciation.text: Ще is one quick syllable, shteh: sh and t together.

translations.en-GB: It's nice weather for a walk

mnemonic.title: Ходя, разходка
mnemonic.text: «Разходка» (a walk) is family with «ходя» (I walk, I go); «раз-» adds “about”: a walk about.

grammar.title: Време, времето
grammar.text: «Време» means both “weather” and “time”. With the suffix, «времето» is “the weather”.

pronunciation.title: The х sound
pronunciation.text: Х is a rough h, as in Scottish “loch”: HOO-ba-vo.

mnemonic.title: Rain chatters on it
mnemonic.text: «Чадър» (umbrella) sounds a bit like “chatter”: picture the rain chattering on it.

grammar.title: «Си»: for yourself
grammar.text: «Си» here means “for yourself”: «вземи си чадър» is “take yourself an umbrella”. «Вземи» is the command to a friend.

pronunciation.title: The vz in вземи
pronunciation.text: Вземи starts with v and z together, no vowel between: vzeh-MEE.

mnemonic.title: Видим, like video
mnemonic.text: «Видим» (we see) shares an ancient root with Latin “video”, I see, which English borrowed.

grammar.title: «Се»: each other
grammar.text: «Се» makes it mutual: «ще се видим» is “we'll see each other”, the usual way to say you'll meet.

pronunciation.title: A tapped р
pronunciation.text: The р in утре is a quick tap of the tongue, not the English r.

phrases.target: Удобно ли ти е в седем?

mnemonic.title: Удобно: comfortable too
mnemonic.text: «Удобно» is “convenient” and also “comfortable”: a comfy chair is «удобен стол».

grammar.title: Ли, ти, е
grammar.text: Short words line up in a fixed order after «удобно»: «ли», then «ти» (to you), then «е» (is).

pronunciation.title: В sounds like f
pronunciation.respelling: oo-DOB-no lee tee eh f SEH-dem
pronunciation.text: Before с, the в is voiceless and sounds like f: f SEH-dem.

translations.en-GB: See you in front of the theatre

mnemonic.title: Театър is theatre
mnemonic.text: «Театър» is “theatre” written in Cyrillic, with ъ in the last syllable: те-а-тър.

grammar.title: Short -а after пред
grammar.text: Masculine nouns take a full «-ът» as the subject and a short «-а» elsewhere: «Театърът е голям», but «пред театъра».

pronunciation.title: teh-A-ta-ra
pronunciation.text: Stress the а after е in театъра, keeping them as two syllables: teh-A-ta-ra.

translations.en-GB: I'll be a bit late, sorry

mnemonic.title: Built on късно
mnemonic.text: «Закъснея» (I'll be late) is built on «късно» (late): literally “to get late”.

grammar.title: Извинявай or извинете
grammar.text: «Извинявай» is “sorry” to a friend. To a stranger, or to several people, say «извинете».

pronunciation.title: The ня in извинявай
pronunciation.text: Ня is like the ny in “canyon”: iz-vee-NYA-vai.

phrases.target: Днес не мога, може би друг ден?

translations.en-GB: I can't today, maybe another day?
translations.ru-RU: Сегодня не могу, может, в другой день?

mnemonic.title: Мога and може би
mnemonic.text: «Може би» (maybe) is built on «може», “it can”: the same verb as «не мога», “I can't”.

grammar.title: «Не» goes first
grammar.text: «Не» goes straight before the verb: «не мога» (I can't). «Мога» turns г into ж in most forms: можеш, може.

pronunciation.title: The dn in днес
pronunciation.ipa: [ˈdnɛs nɛ ˈmɔɡɐ ˈmɔʒɛ bi ˈdruɡ ˈdɛn]
pronunciation.respelling: DNES neh MO-ga, MO-zheh bee DROOG DEN
pronunciation.text: Днес starts with d and n together, no vowel between: DNES.

translations.en-GB: Where do I check in my luggage?

mnemonic.title: “Check in” in Bulgarian
mnemonic.text: «Чекирам» is just English “check” with the verb ending «-ирам», as in «паркирам», “to park”.

grammar.title: Full article «-ът»
grammar.text: A masculine noun takes «-ът» when it is the subject: «багажът». Elsewhere it takes «-а»: «чекирам багажа».

pronunciation.title: The «-ът» ending
pronunciation.text: Final «-ът» has a short, neutral vowel, like the a in “about”.

mnemonic.title: The «лет» family
mnemonic.text: «Полет» is built on «лет-», “fly”: an airport is a «летище» and a plane a «самолет», a “self-flyer”.

grammar.title: «Ми» after the noun
grammar.text: The short «ми» (my) follows the noun, which takes “the”: «полетът ми», literally “the flight my”.

pronunciation.title: PO-let
pronunciation.text: Stress the first syllable of «полет»: PO-let.

phrases.target: Кой е изходът за моя полет?

mnemonic.title: Out + going
mnemonic.text: «Изход» is «из» (out) + «ход» (going): the way out. At an airport it is also the gate.

grammar.title: “The” goes on «моя»
grammar.text: The definite ending goes on the first word: «мой» → «моя полет», not «моя полетът». «Полетът ми» says the same.

pronunciation.title: «З» turns to s
pronunciation.respelling: KOY eh EES-ho-dut zuh MO-yuh PO-let
pronunciation.text: Before «х», the «з» of «изход» loses its voice and sounds like s: EES-hot.

mnemonic.title: «Късно» means late
mnemonic.text: «Закъснява» is built on «късно», “late”: the flight is running late.

grammar.title: Ongoing: «закъснява»
grammar.text: «Закъснява» is imperfective, for a delay still going on. The perfective past says it was late: «полетът закъсня».

pronunciation.title: Stress on «ня»
pronunciation.text: Stress «ня» in «закъснява», with a soft n, like the ny in “canyon”.

mnemonic.title: Arrive means reach
mnemonic.text: «Пристигна» is built on «стигам», “to reach”: «при-» + reach gives “arrive”. Arrivals boards say «Пристигащи».

grammar.title: Past: «пристигна»
grammar.text: «Пристигна» is the aorist, the everyday past for a finished event. «Не» goes straight before the verb.

pronunciation.title: KOO-far
pronunciation.text: Stress the first syllable of «куфар», and keep the unstressed «а» short, like the a in “about”.

mnemonic.title: Lending your «мощ»
mnemonic.text: «Помощ» holds «мощ», “strength”, from the same root as «мога», “I can”: help is lending your strength.

grammar.title: Noun or command
grammar.text: «Помощ!» is the noun, the usual shout. To ask someone directly: «Помогнете ми!» (polite or plural), «Помогни ми!» (to a friend).

pronunciation.title: «Щ» is “sht”
pronunciation.text: «Щ» is sh and t together: PO-mosht.

mnemonic.title: «Вик» is a shout
mnemonic.text: «Извикайте» is built on «вик», “a shout”: «викам» is to call out, and «извикам» to summon someone.

grammar.title: Polite «-йте»
grammar.text: «Извикайте» is the polite command (вие): «-йте» on the stem. To a friend: «Извикай линейка!».

pronunciation.title: A soft «ля»
pronunciation.text: «Ля» in «моля» has a soft l, like the lli in “million”.

mnemonic.title: Carrying sheets of paper
mnemonic.text: «Портфейл» comes from French “portefeuille”, “carry leaves”, the same idea as English “portfolio”.

grammar.title: An unnamed “they”
grammar.text: «Откраднаха» (“they stole”) leaves the thief unnamed. «Ми» (to me) marks who lost it: “they stole my wallet”.

pronunciation.title: The «х» sound
pronunciation.text: «Х» is like the ch in Scottish “loch”, never silent like English h.

translations.en-GB: Where is the nearest police station?

mnemonic.title: Близо, близнак
mnemonic.text: «Близко» is from «близо», “near”; a twin is a «близнак», the one nearest to you.

grammar.title: «Най-» means “most”
grammar.text: Add «най-» with a hyphen for “most”: «близко» → «най-близкото», “the nearest”. “The” goes on this first word.

pronunciation.title: Two stresses
pronunciation.text: «Най-» has its own stress, and so does the word after it: NAY-BLEES-ko-to.

mnemonic.title: Gobbled up by the city
mnemonic.text: Hear «губ» in «изгубих» as “gobble”: picture the city gobbling you up. «Изгубих се», I’m lost.

grammar.title: Where «се» goes
grammar.text: «Се» can't open a sentence, so it follows the verb: «изгубих се». After another word it comes first: «Май се изгубих».

pronunciation.title: Stress on «гу»
pronunciation.text: Stress «гу», and don't drop the final «х»: it's the ch of Scottish “loch”.

translations.en-GB: I have a meeting at ten

mnemonic.title: Face to face
mnemonic.text: «Среща» shares its root with «срещу», “opposite, facing”: a meeting puts people face to face.

grammar.title: «В» for clock times
grammar.text: Clock times take «в»: «в десет», «в пет и половина».

pronunciation.title: A one-letter «в»
pronunciation.text: «В» is a word with no vowel: join it to the next one, “vDEH-set”.

phrases.target: Може ли да ми изпратиш доклада?

translations.en-GB: Can you send me the report?

mnemonic.title: «Пратка», a parcel
mnemonic.text: «Изпратиш» is built on «пратя», “send”: a «пратка» is a parcel, something sent.

grammar.title: No infinitive: «да»
grammar.text: Bulgarian has no infinitive: “can you send” is «може ли да» + a present-tense verb: «да ми изпратиш».

pronunciation.title: The «ж» sound
pronunciation.respelling: MO-zheh lee duh mee ees-PRAH-teesh dok-LAH-duh
pronunciation.text: «Ж» in «може» is the s of “pleasure”.

translations.en-GB: I work from home on Fridays
translations.ru-RU: По пятницам я работаю из дома

mnemonic.title: Five for Friday
mnemonic.text: «Петък» comes from «пет», “five”: Friday is the fifth day, counting from Monday.

grammar.title: «Вкъщи» and «от вкъщи»
grammar.text: «Вкъщи» means both “at home” and “home” (where to). “From home” adds «от»: «от вкъщи».

pronunciation.title: «В» sounds like f
pronunciation.text: Before a voiceless sound, «в» is said as f: «в петък» is “f PEH-tuk”, and «вкъщи» is “FKUSH-tee”.

mnemonic.title: A little minute
mnemonic.text: «Минутка» is «минута» with the small, friendly ending «-ка»: “a quick minute”.

grammar.title: Ти or вие
grammar.text: «Имаш» is the ти form, for colleagues you know well. To a manager or a stranger: «Имате ли минутка?».

pronunciation.title: Stress on «ну»
pronunciation.text: Stress «ну»: mi-NOOT-ka. The final «а» is short and light, like the a in “about”.

mnemonic.title: To the top
mnemonic.text: «Довърша» shares its root with «връх», “top, peak”: to finish a job is to bring it to the top.

grammar.title: Future with «ще»
grammar.text: «Ще» makes the future, and the short «го» (it) goes between «ще» and the verb: «ще го довърша».

pronunciation.title: A stressed «ъ»
pronunciation.text: The stressed «ъ» in «довърша» is a full vowel, close to the u in British “hurt”.

mnemonic.title: A word to get in
mnemonic.text: «Парола» comes from French parole, “word”: a password is the word that lets you in.

grammar.title: Short “the” after «за»
grammar.text: After a preposition a masculine noun takes the short “the”, «-а»: «за интернета». As the subject it's «интернетът».

pronunciation.title: in-ter-NE-ta
pronunciation.text: Bulgarian stresses the end of «интернет», in-ter-NET, so «интернета» is in-ter-NE-ta.

mnemonic.title: The battery fell
mnemonic.text: Bulgarian says the battery “fell”: «падна» means “it fell”, like a charge bar dropping to zero.

grammar.title: «Ми» after the noun
grammar.text: «Ми» (my) comes after the noun, and the noun keeps its “the”: «батерията ми», literally “the battery of me”.

pronunciation.title: ba-TE-ri-ya-ta
pronunciation.text: Stress the second syllable of «батерията», not the end: ba-TE-ri-ya-ta.

phrases.target: Мога ли да си заредя телефона тук?

translations.en-GB: Can I charge my phone here?

mnemonic.title: Charge, load, refuel
mnemonic.text: «Заредя» also means “to load” or “to refuel”: you fill the phone up, as you'd fill up a car.

grammar.title: No infinitive: «да»
grammar.text: Bulgarian has no infinitive: “can I charge” is «мога да заредя», literally “I can that I charge”.

pronunciation.title: za-re-DYA
pronunciation.ipa: [ˈmɔɡɐ li dɐ si zɐrɛˈdʲa tɛlɛˈfɔnɐ ˈtuk]
pronunciation.respelling: MO-ga lee da see za-reh-DYA teh-leh-FO-na TOOK
pronunciation.text: «Дя» is a d with a y-glide, and it takes the stress: za-re-DYA.

mnemonic.title: «Ще» once meant “want”
mnemonic.text: «Ще» comes from an old verb meaning “want”, just as English “will” once did. Put it before a verb for the future.

grammar.title: Little words in order
grammar.text: The short words go in a fixed order before the verb: «ще» (will), «ти» (to you), then «се»: «ще ти се обадя».

pronunciation.title: Щ is sht
pronunciation.text: Bulgarian «щ» is “sht”, so «ще» sounds like “shteh”.

mnemonic.title: Не + имам = нямам
mnemonic.text: «Нямам» was once «не» + «имам» (“I have”) run together: “I have not”. «Няма» likewise means “there isn't”.

grammar.title: No «аз» needed
grammar.text: The verb ending shows who: «-м» is “I”, so «нямам» alone means “I haven't got”, without «аз» (“I”).

pronunciation.title: NYA-mam
pronunciation.text: «Ня» is a soft n, like the ny in “canyon”, and it takes the stress.

mnemonic.title: Сестра and “sister”
mnemonic.text: «Сестра» and “sister” come from the same ancient root; you can hear s, t and r in both.

grammar.title: Usually no “a”
grammar.text: Bulgarian usually needs no word for “a”: «имам сестра» is simply “I have sister”.

pronunciation.title: ses-TRA
pronunciation.text: Stress the last syllable of «сестра»: ses-TRA.

mnemonic.title: Дете, деца
mnemonic.text: One child is «дете»; the plural changes its ending, «деца», much like “child” and “children”.

grammar.title: Ти or вие
grammar.text: «Имаш» is the «ти» form, for a friend. To someone you'd address as «вие»: «Имате ли деца?».

pronunciation.title: de-TSA
pronunciation.text: Stress the end of «деца»: de-TSA. «Ц» is ts, as in “cats”.

translations.en-GB: My parents live in the countryside

mnemonic.title: Parents, birth, birthday
mnemonic.text: «Родители» (parents) shares its root with «роден» (born) and «рожден ден» (birthday): the people you were born to.

grammar.title: Plural “the” is «-те»
grammar.text: Plurals ending in «-и» add «-те» for “the”: «родители» (parents) → «родителите» (the parents), then «ми».

pronunciation.title: An unstressed o stays o
pronunciation.text: The unstressed «о» of «родителите» stays a clear o: ro-DI-te-li-te, never “ra-”.

phrases.target: Синът ми е на пет години

mnemonic.title: Син: son, and blue
mnemonic.text: «Син» is a distant cousin of “son”. The same word also means “blue”, so context tells them apart.

grammar.title: Age with «на»
grammar.text: Bulgarian gives age with «на»: «е на пет години», literally “is at five years”. «Години» is often dropped: «той е на пет».

pronunciation.title: Stress moves: si-NUHT
pronunciation.respelling: see-NUHT mee eh na PET go-DEE-nee
pronunciation.text: With “the”, the stress moves onto the ending: «син», but «синът», si-NUHT.

mnemonic.title: A family man
mnemonic.text: «Семейство» shares its root with «семеен» (“with a family”): a «семеен човек» is a family man.

grammar.title: Neuter “the” is «-то»
grammar.text: Neuter nouns in «-о» add «-то» for “the”: «семейство» → «семейството». «Ти» (your) then follows.

pronunciation.title: se-MEY-stvo-to
pronunciation.text: Stress «мей», which rhymes with “may”: se-MEY-stvo-to.

phrases.target: Искам да запазя маса за четирима

translations.en-GB: I'd like to book a table for four

mnemonic.title: Keep a table
mnemonic.text: «Запазя» means “to keep” or “to save”: you're asking them to keep a table for you.

grammar.title: Numbers for people
grammar.text: Bulgarian counts men or mixed groups with special numbers: «двама», «трима», «четирима». Things take «четири».

pronunciation.title: che-ti-REE-ma
pronunciation.respelling: EES-kam da za-PA-zya MA-sa za che-tee-REE-ma
pronunciation.text: Stress «ри» in «четирима»: che-ti-REE-ma, unlike «четири» (CHE-ti-ri).

phrases.target: Имате ли свободна маса за довечера?

translations.en-GB: Do you have a table free for tonight?
translations.ru-RU: У вас есть свободный столик на сегодня вечером?

mnemonic.title: До + вечер
mnemonic.text: «Довечера» is «до» (“until”) + «вечер» (“evening”): later this evening, so “tonight”.

grammar.title: «Свободна» matches «маса»
grammar.text: Adjectives agree with the noun: «маса» is feminine, so «свободна»; a free seat is «свободно място».

pronunciation.title: do-VE-che-ra
pronunciation.respelling: EE-ma-teh lee svo-BOD-na MA-sa za do-VEH-che-ra
pronunciation.text: Stress the second syllable of «довечера»: do-VE-che-ra.

translations.en-GB: Whose name is the booking under?

mnemonic.title: -tion becomes «-ция»
mnemonic.text: «Резервация» is “reservation”: English -tion often turns into Bulgarian «-ция», as in «информация» and «станция».

grammar.title: “Whose” matches the noun
grammar.text: “Whose” agrees with the thing owned: «чий» (m), «чия» (f), «чие» (n). «Име» is neuter, so «чие име».

pronunciation.title: Two syllables in «чие»
pronunciation.text: «Чие» has two syllables, CHEE-eh, with the stress on the first.

mnemonic.title: Навън and вътре
mnemonic.text: «Навън» (outside) pairs with «вътре» (inside); on its own, «вън!» means “out!”.

grammar.title: Asking with «може ли»
grammar.text: «Може ли да…?» (“is it possible to…?”) plus a verb in any person is the easy polite request: «може ли да седнем».

pronunciation.title: The stressed ъ
pronunciation.text: The stressed «ъ» of «навън» is like the u in “hurt”, without the r.

translations.en-GB: We have to cancel the booking

mnemonic.title: A family of changes
mnemonic.text: «Отменя» (to cancel) is kin to «сменя» (to swap) and «променя» (to change): «от-» takes the plan away.

grammar.title: «Трябва» never changes
grammar.text: «Трябва» (must) stays the same for everyone: «трябва да отменя», «трябва да отменим». The person shows on the next verb.

pronunciation.title: TRYAB-va
pronunciation.text: «Ря» in «трябва» is an r with a y-glide: TRYAB-va.

mnemonic.title: Chemist, as in chemistry
mnemonic.text: «Chemist» belongs to the «chemistry» family. In Britain it also names the shop (often «chemist's») where you buy medicine, and the pharmacist who works there; «pharmacy» is understood too.

grammar.title: «The nearest»: adjective + -est
grammar.text: «Where's» is «where is». A short adjective makes its superlative with «-est»: «near» → «the nearest». Always put «the» before a superlative: «the nearest chemist».

pronunciation.title: Ch is a k
pronunciation.text: The «ch» of «chemist» is a «k», as in «chemistry», not the «ch» of «cheese». The stress is on the first syllable: KEM-ist.

phrases.target: Have you got anything for a cough?

translations.ru-RU: У вас есть что-нибудь от кашля?

mnemonic.title: Cough sounds like a cough
mnemonic.text: Say «cough» out loud and you can hear the cough in it: «kof». The spelling is the odd part, so remember the sound first and the letters second.

grammar.title: «Have you got» and «anything»
grammar.text: «Have you got…?» is the everyday British way to ask «Do you have…?», and it needs no «do». In a question, «anything» is the usual word. An illness takes «a»: «a cough», «a cold».

pronunciation.title: The f of cough, the th of anything
pronunciation.ipa: [həv ju ˈɡɒt ˈen.i.θɪŋ fər ə ˈkɒf]
pronunciation.respelling: huv yoo GOT EN-ee-thing fer uh KOF
pronunciation.text: «Cough» ends in an «f», like «off»: «kof». The «gh» is not read. The «th» in «anything» is the breathy one: tongue lightly between the teeth, with no «s» and no «t».

phrases.target: I've had a headache since this morning

translations.ru-RU: У меня с утра болит голова

mnemonic.title: Head + ache
mnemonic.text: «Headache» is just «head» + «ache» (pain), built like «toothache» and «earache». Learn «ache» once and you can name pains all over the body.

grammar.title: «I've had… since»
grammar.text: For something that began in the past and is still true, English uses the present perfect: «I've had…», not «I have… since». Use «since» with a starting point (this morning, Monday) and «for» with a length of time (for two days).

pronunciation.title: «Ache» rhymes with «cake»
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪv hæd ə ˈhed.eɪk sɪns ðɪs ˈmɔː.nɪŋ]
pronunciation.respelling: ai-v had uh HED-ayk sinss thiss MOR-ning
pronunciation.text: The «ache» in «headache» is «ayk», rhyming with «cake»: the «ch» is a «k», not a «ch». Stress the first syllable: HED-ayk.

mnemonic.title: Words you already know
mnemonic.text: Both long words are international and probably exist in your own language too, so you already know them. Only the stress is new.

grammar.title: «Allergic to»
grammar.text: «Allergic» is an adjective, so it goes with «I'm» and takes «to»: «allergic to penicillin», «allergic to nuts». The noun is «allergy»: «a penicillin allergy».

pronunciation.title: The g is a j
pronunciation.text: In «allergic» the «g» sounds like the «j» in «jam», and the stress is on «ler»: uh-LUR-jik. In «penicillin» it falls on «cil»: pen-i-SIL-in.

phrases.target: I'd like an appointment with a GP, please

translations.bg-BG: Може ли да запиша час при личен лекар, моля?
translations.ru-RU: Мне бы записаться на приём к терапевту, пожалуйста

mnemonic.title: GP: your first doctor
mnemonic.text: «GP» stands for «general practitioner», the family doctor you see first in Britain, before any specialist. Say the letters aloud, «jee-pee», and picture the doctor around the corner.

grammar.title: «I'd like», «a» and «an»
grammar.text: «I'd like» (I would like) is the polite way to ask; «I want» sounds blunt. The article follows the sound, not the spelling: «an appointment» (vowel sound), but «a GP» (it starts with the consonant sound «j»).

pronunciation.title: Stress: uh-POINT-ment
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪd ˈlaɪk ən əˈpɔɪnt.mənt wɪð ə ˌdʒiːˈpiː pliːz]
pronunciation.respelling: ai-d LIKE un uh-POINT-ment with uh jee-PEE, pleez
pronunciation.text: Stress the middle syllable: uh-POINT-ment, with «oy» as in «boy». The first syllable is a weak «uh», not «ap».

phrases.target: I've booked a double room for two nights

translations.bg-BG: Имам резервация за двойна стая за две нощи
translations.ru-RU: У меня забронирован двухместный номер на две ночи

mnemonic.title: Booking.com in a sentence
mnemonic.text: You may know «Booking.com»: «to book» is the verb for reserving. The same word as «book» (the thing you read) is also a verb: «I've booked a room» means «I've made a booking».

grammar.title: «I've booked»: done, and it matters now
grammar.text: The present perfect «I've booked» links a past action to now: the room is booked, and that matters at the desk. «For two nights» gives the length: «for» + a period of time.

pronunciation.title: «Booked» is one syllable
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪv ˈbʊkt ə ˈdʌb.l̩ ruːm fə tuː ˈnaɪts]
pronunciation.respelling: ai-v BOOKT uh DUB-ul room fuh too NITES
pronunciation.text: After a «k» the «-ed» sounds like «t»: «booked» is «bookt», one syllable, with a short «oo» as in «good». Don't say «boo-ked».

mnemonic.title: Break + fast
mnemonic.text: «Breakfast» is «break» + «fast»: the meal that breaks the long fast of the night. This «fast» means not eating, not speed.

grammar.title: The passive: «is served»
grammar.text: Breakfast doesn't serve anyone; it is served by the hotel. The passive is «is/are» + past participle: «is served», «are included». The question words come first, with no «do»: «What time is breakfast served?»

pronunciation.title: BREK-fust, not break-fast
pronunciation.text: The «ea» is short, as in «bed», and the stress is on the first syllable: BREK-fust. The last syllable is weak, so «fast» is not said like the word «fast».

phrases.target: Could I have an extra towel, please?

translations.bg-BG: Може ли още една хавлия, моля?

mnemonic.title: An international word
mnemonic.text: «Extra» is an international word you probably use already. The same frame, «Could I have an extra…?», fits a pillow, a blanket, a hanger or a key.

grammar.title: «Could I have…?» and «an»
grammar.text: «Could I have…?» is the polite British way to ask for something, softer than «I want». Use «an» before a vowel sound: «an extra towel», but «a towel».

pronunciation.title: Silent l, and a two-beat towel
pronunciation.ipa: [kʊd aɪ həv ən ˈek.strə ˈtaʊ.əl pliːz]
pronunciation.respelling: kood ai huv un EK-struh TOW-ul pleez
pronunciation.text: The «l» in «could» is silent: «kood», with a short «oo». «Towel» has two beats, TOW-ul, with «ow» as in «cow», not «toe-el».

phrases.target: There's no hot water in my room

translations.bg-BG: В стаята ми няма топла вода
translations.ru-RU: В моём номере нет горячей воды

mnemonic.title: Hot, as in hot dog
mnemonic.text: «Hot» is the first word of «hot dog», a sausage served hot. Picture yourself under a cold shower, then say «no hot water».

grammar.title: «There's no…»
grammar.text: «There's no…» (there is no) says something is missing: «There's no hot water», «There's no Wi-Fi». Add the place with «in»: «in my room». Don't say «I haven't hot water».

pronunciation.title: Rounded w, soft h
pronunciation.ipa: [ðeəz ˈnəʊ ˈhɒt ˈwɔː.tə ɪn maɪ ˈruːm]
pronunciation.respelling: thairz NOH HOT WOR-tuh in my ROOM
pronunciation.text: In «water» the «w» is made with rounded lips and no contact with the teeth: «w», not «v». The «h» of «hot» is a soft breath, with no scrape in the throat.

phrases.target: Can we leave our bags here after check-out?

translations.bg-BG: Може ли да оставим багажа си тук, след като освободим стаята?
translations.ru-RU: Можно оставить багаж здесь после выезда?

mnemonic.title: Check-out is a word you know
mnemonic.text: Booking sites use «check-in» and «check-out» everywhere, so you may know them already. «Bags» is the everyday word for luggage.

grammar.title: «Can we» + plain verb, «after» + noun
grammar.text: After «can» comes the plain verb with no «to»: «Can we leave…?». «After» is a preposition, so a noun or an -ing form follows: «after check-out», «after checking out».

pronunciation.title: Short a and a voiced z in «bags»
pronunciation.ipa: [kən wi ˈliːv aʊə ˈbæɡz hɪər ˈɑːf.tə ˈtʃek.aʊt]
pronunciation.respelling: kun wee LEEV ow-uh BAGZ heer AHF-tuh CHEK-owt
pronunciation.text: «Bags» has the short «a» of «cat», and its last sound is a «z»: «bagz». Keep the «g» voiced; don't harden it into a «k» at the end.

phrases.target: Do you have this in a medium?

translations.bg-BG: Имате ли това в среден размер?
translations.ru-RU: У вас есть это в среднем размере?

mnemonic.title: Medium = middle
mnemonic.text: «Medium» comes from the Latin word for «middle», like «Mediterranean» («in the middle of the land»). It's the size between «small» and «large»: tags say S, M or L.

grammar.title: «In» for size and colour
grammar.text: Say «in» for size and colour: «in a medium», «in black», «in a smaller size». «Do you have…?» asks whether the shop has it.

pronunciation.title: Th in «this», long ee in «medium»
pronunciation.ipa: [də ju ˈhæv ðɪs ɪn ə ˈmiː.di.əm]
pronunciation.respelling: duh yoo HAV this in uh MEE-dee-um
pronunciation.text: In «this» the «th» is voiced: tongue lightly between the teeth, not «z» or «d», and the «i» is short. «Medium» starts with a long «ee»: MEE-dee-um.

mnemonic.title: Try it ON
mnemonic.text: Picture the shirt going ON your shoulders: you «try» it «on». That little word «on» is the whole idea, so keep it at the end.

grammar.title: «Try on»: pronoun in the middle
grammar.text: «Try on» is a phrasal verb. A pronoun goes between its two parts: «try it on», «try them on», never «try on it». A noun can go either side: «try on this shirt» or «try this shirt on».

pronunciation.title: Weak «can»
pronunciation.text: In «Can I try this on?» the word «can» is weak, almost «kn», and the stress lands on «try» and «on». The «th» in «this» is the voiced one: tongue lightly between the teeth.

mnemonic.title: A room to change in
mnemonic.text: A «changing room» is simply a room to «change» in: one set of clothes off, another on. Shops say «fitting room» too, but «changing room» is the usual British word.

grammar.title: «Where are» with plurals
grammar.text: «Are» goes with plural nouns: «Where are the changing rooms?», but «Where is the changing room?». In «changing room» the -ing word says what the room is for, as in «waiting room» and «dining room».

pronunciation.title: «-ing» is one nasal sound
pronunciation.text: The «ng» of «changing» is one sound made at the back of the mouth, with no separate «g» or «k» after it. Say CHAYN-jing, with the «j» of «jam» in the middle.

phrases.target: It's a bit tight, I'm afraid

mnemonic.title: «I'm afraid» cushions bad news
mnemonic.text: «I'm afraid» doesn't mean you are scared. It puts a soft cushion under bad news, like «I'm sorry to say». Picture yourself handing back a jacket with a gentle smile.

grammar.title: «A bit» softens
grammar.text: «A bit» + adjective makes a complaint gentler: «a bit tight», «a bit big», «a bit short». British speakers understate, so «a bit tight» may mean quite tight.

pronunciation.title: Short i in «bit»
pronunciation.respelling: its uh BIT TITE, ai-m uh-FRAYD
pronunciation.text: The «i» in «bit» is short and relaxed, quite different from the long «ee» of «beat»: a «bit» is small, a «beat» is a drum. Say «bit» quickly, without lengthening it.

mnemonic.title: «Sale» sounds like «sail»
mnemonic.text: You've seen «SALE» in shop windows everywhere. Say it «sayl», like the «sail» of a boat: the two words sound identical.

grammar.title: «In the sale»
grammar.text: In Britain, goods with reduced prices are «in the sale»: «Is this in the sale?». «On sale» is the usual American wording. «The sale» is the whole period of reductions.

pronunciation.title: Two voiced th's
pronunciation.text: «This» and «the» both start with the voiced «th»: tongue lightly between the teeth, not «z» or «d». «Sale» has the «ay» of «day» and rhymes with «tail».

mnemonic.title: Say «do» twice
mnemonic.text: Tap it out on two fingers: «What DO you DO?». The first «do» is only a helper; the second one means «work as». The question asks about your job or your studies.

grammar.title: Job or right now?
grammar.text: «What do you do?» (present simple) asks about your regular job. «What are you doing?» (present continuous) asks what you are doing right now. A good answer is «I'm a nurse» or «I work in a bank».

pronunciation.title: W is not v
pronunciation.text: The «w» in «what» is made with rounded lips and no contact with the teeth: «wot», not «vot». The vowel is a short, rounded «o».

mnemonic.title: A long queue
mnemonic.text: Picture a long bus queue and ask the person next to you: «Have you been here long?». The word «long» carries the whole question, so you needn't say «a long time».

grammar.title: Present perfect for “so far”
grammar.text: To ask how long someone has been somewhere up to now, English uses the present perfect: «Have you been here long?», not «Are you here long?». «Long» alone works in questions and negatives; in positive sentences say «a long time» or «for two weeks».

pronunciation.title: A soft h
pronunciation.text: The «h» in «have» and «here» is a soft breath, like fogging a mirror, with no scrape in the throat. In «long» the «ng» is one nasal sound, with no hard «g» after it.

mnemonic.title: A holy day off
mnemonic.text: «Holiday» began as «holy day»: a special day off. In Britain it now means a whole trip or time away from work, what Americans call «vacation».

grammar.title: «On holiday», not «in»
grammar.text: It is a fixed phrase: «on holiday», «on business», «on a trip». Not «in holiday» or «at holiday». The question is made with «Are you…?», with no «do».

pronunciation.title: HOL-i-day: stress the first syllable
pronunciation.text: Stress the first syllable: HOL-i-day, with a short, round «o» and a weak middle. Don't stress the end, as in «holi-DAY». The «h» is a soft breath.

phrases.target: Sorry, my English isn't very good

translations.bg-BG: Съжалявам, английският ми не е много добър
translations.ru-RU: Извините, у меня не очень хороший английский

mnemonic.title: Start with «sorry»
mnemonic.text: Open with «Sorry,» the way Britons do before almost anything awkward: it sounds friendly, not weak. Picture yourself smiling as you say it, and the rest of the sentence follows.

grammar.title: «Good» or «well»?
grammar.text: After «my English is…» use an adjective: «good», «not very good». With the verb «speak» use an adverb: «I speak English well». «Isn't» is «is not».

pronunciation.title: ING-glish
pronunciation.respelling: SOR-ee, my ING-glish IZ-unt VEH-ree GOOD
pronunciation.text: «English» starts with a short «i», as in «bit», not «e»: ING-glish. The «ng» is followed by a clear «g»; compare «singer», where the «g» is silent.

mnemonic.title: Know-how, reversed
mnemonic.text: «Know-how» is a loanword in many languages, so you may already know the pair. This question just puts the two words the other way round: «How do you know…?»

grammar.title: «How», not «where from»
grammar.text: English most often asks «How do you know…?», because the answer is a connection: «We work together», «She's my cousin». «Know» is a state verb, so it stays in the simple present: «do you know», not «are you knowing».

pronunciation.title: The k in «know» is silent
pronunciation.text: «Know» sounds exactly like «no»: the «k» is silent. In «how» the «h» is a soft breath and «ow» is the sound in «cow».

mnemonic.title: Supposed = presumed
mnemonic.text: «Supposed» means «presumed»: the forecast presumes rain. Picture the TV weatherman pointing at a cloud and saying «it's supposed to rain later»: expected, not certain.

grammar.title: «Be supposed to» = expected
