grammar.text: «Be supposed to» + verb says what is expected, often from a forecast or a timetable: «It's supposed to rain», «The shop is supposed to open at nine». It is less sure than «It will rain».

pronunciation.title: «Supposed to» runs together
pronunciation.text: «Supposed to» is said as one word, suh-POHS-tuh: the «d» disappears and «to» is a weak «tuh». The «-er» of «later» is a plain «uh», with no «r».

mnemonic.title: Fore + cast
mnemonic.text: «Fore-» means «before», as in «foresee», and «cast» means «throw»: a forecast is a guess thrown forward in time.

grammar.title: «The forecast for…»
grammar.text: «What's» is «what is». «For» says which day the forecast covers: «for tomorrow», «for the weekend». «Tomorrow» needs no «on» or «in».

pronunciation.title: FORE-cast, to-MOR-row
pronunciation.text: «Forecast» is stressed on the first syllable, FOR-kahst, with a long «ah» in British English. In «tomorrow» the stress is on «mor»: tuh-MOR-oh.

mnemonic.title: Freezer weather
mnemonic.text: «Freezing» is the «-ing» form of «freeze», the verb inside «freezer». Imagine stepping outside into an open freezer.

grammar.title: Weather needs «it»
grammar.text: An English statement needs a subject, so weather talk starts with «it»: «It's freezing», «It's raining», «It's sunny». Don't leave «it» out.

pronunciation.title: Voiced z and th
pronunciation.text: The middle of «freezing» is a voiced «z», not «s», and the «ee» is long. In «there» the «th» is voiced: tongue lightly between the teeth, not «d» or «z».

mnemonic.title: Hot as a kettle
mnemonic.text: Water is at its hottest when it's boiling, so on a very hot day Britons say it's «boiling», just as they say «freezing» for very cold. Picture a whistling kettle.

grammar.title: «Really boiling», not «very»
grammar.text: «Boiling» already means «very hot», so it takes «really» or «absolutely», not «very»: «really boiling». The same goes for «freezing», «huge» and «exhausted».

pronunciation.title: The English r is not rolled
pronunciation.text: The «r» in «really» is not rolled: the tongue tip curls back without touching anything, and the lips round a little. «Boiling» has the «oy» of «boy».

mnemonic.title: A little shade
mnemonic.text: «Umbrella» goes back to the Latin word for «shade», «umbra»: it is literally a little shade you carry over your head.

grammar.title: «You'd better» + plain verb
grammar.text: «You'd better» (you had better) gives strong advice: do it, or something bad may happen. It is followed by the plain verb, with no «to»: «You'd better take…», «You'd better not forget».

pronunciation.title: um-BREL-uh: stress in the middle
pronunciation.text: «Umbrella» is stressed on the second syllable: um-BREL-uh. The first syllable is short and weak, with the «u» of «cup», and the last is a weak «uh».

translations.ru-RU: У тебя есть время в эти выходные?

mnemonic.title: Free = empty in the diary
mnemonic.text: «Free» means «not busy» as well as «costing nothing». Picture a diary with nothing written in the weekend: that weekend is «free».

grammar.title: No preposition before «this weekend»
grammar.text: Words like «this», «next» and «last» do the work of a preposition: «this weekend», «next week», «last night». Don't add «in» or «on».

pronunciation.title: Week-END
pronunciation.text: In «weekend» the main stress is on the second part: week-END. The «w» is made with rounded lips: «week» starts like «we», not «ve».

phrases.target: Do you fancy going for a drink?

translations.bg-BG: Искаш ли да пийнем по нещо?

mnemonic.title: Fancy comes from fantasy
mnemonic.text: «Fancy» is a short form of «fantasy». If you «fancy» something, it catches your imagination: you feel like it. In Britain, «a drink» often means a pint or a glass out.

grammar.title: «Fancy» + noun or -ing
grammar.text: As a verb, «fancy» means «feel like» and takes a noun or an -ing form: «Do you fancy a drink?», «Do you fancy going out?», not «fancy to go». With a person it means «be attracted to», so «Do you fancy Sam?» is a different question.

pronunciation.title: Open a in «fancy»
pronunciation.ipa: [də ju ˈfæn.si ˈɡəʊ.ɪŋ fər ə ˈdrɪŋk]
pronunciation.respelling: duh yoo FAN-see GOH-ing fer uh DRINK
pronunciation.text: The «a» in «fancy» is the open vowel of «cat»: jaw low, between «e» and «a». In «going» the vowel glides, GOH-ing: it isn't a pure «o».

phrases.target: Let's meet outside the cinema at half six

translations.bg-BG: Да се срещнем пред киното в шест и половина
translations.ru-RU: Давай встретимся у кинотеатра в половине седьмого

mnemonic.title: Cinema, short for cinematograph
mnemonic.text: «Cinema» shares its root with «kino» in Bulgarian and Russian: both are short for «cinematograph». In Britain you go to the cinema; Americans say «movie theater».

grammar.title: «Half six» means 6.30
grammar.text: Britons say «half six» for 6.30: it's short for «half past six», and it never means 5.30. With clock times use «at»: «at half six», «at seven». «Let's» + plain verb makes a suggestion.

pronunciation.title: Silent l in «half»
pronunciation.ipa: [ˈlets ˈmiːt aʊtˈsaɪd ðə ˈsɪn.ə.mə ət ˈhɑːf ˈsɪks]
pronunciation.respelling: LETS MEET owt-SIDE thuh SIN-uh-muh at HAHF SIX
pronunciation.text: The «l» in «half» is silent: «hahf», with a long «ah». Stress «cinema» on the first syllable: SIN-uh-muh, not «ci-NE-ma».

phrases.target: I'm running a bit late, sorry

mnemonic.title: Running after the clock
mnemonic.text: Picture someone sprinting down the street with one eye on a watch: that's «running late». It's an idiom, so learn the whole chunk together.

grammar.title: «I'm running late»: still on my way
grammar.text: The present continuous «I'm running late» describes what's happening now and warns of a delay: you are on your way and will arrive late. «I'm late» says you are already late.

pronunciation.title: The u of «cup» in «running»
pronunciation.respelling: ai-m RUN-ing uh BIT LAYT SOR-ee
pronunciation.text: «Running» has the short, relaxed «u» of «cup»: RUN-ing, closer to «a» than to «o». The ending is one nasal «ng», with no «g».

phrases.target: I can't make it on Friday. How about Saturday?

translations.bg-BG: В петък не мога. Какво ще кажеш за събота?
translations.ru-RU: В пятницу не получится. А как насчёт субботы?

mnemonic.title: Saturn's day
mnemonic.text: «Saturday» is «Saturn's day»: it begins just like the planet Saturn, named after the same Roman god. Picture the ringed planet hanging over your plans for the weekend.

grammar.title: «On» with days
grammar.text: Use «on» before a day: «on Friday», «on Saturday» (and «at» before a clock time: «at seven»). «Make it» means manage to come, and «How about…?» suggests an alternative.

pronunciation.title: Long ah in «can't»
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪ ˈkɑːnt ˈmeɪk ɪt ɒn ˈfraɪ.deɪ ˈhaʊ əˌbaʊt ˈsæt.ə.deɪ]
pronunciation.respelling: ai KAHNT MAYK it on FRY-day. HOW uh-BOWT SAT-uh-day
pronunciation.text: In British English «can't» has a long «ah», KAHNT, and a clear final «t», while «can» is a quick «kn». That long vowel is how listeners tell «I can't» from «I can».

phrases.target: Where do I check in, please?

mnemonic.title: You already know «check-in»
mnemonic.text: The word is probably in your own language already, from airport signs and apps. Picture the desk with that sign above it, then put «Where do I…?» in front.

grammar.title: Questions with «do»
grammar.text: After «where», the question needs «do» before the subject: «Where do I check in?». The main verb stays in its base form, with no ending.

pronunciation.title: A voiced z in «please»
pronunciation.respelling: WAIR duh eye CHEK in, PLEEZ
pronunciation.text: Keep your voice on to the very end of «please»: it finishes with z, not s. Bulgarian and Russian both let final consonants go quiet, so listen for the buzz.

phrases.target: Has the gate been announced yet?

mnemonic.title: Waiting at the empty gate
mnemonic.text: Picture the departures board with the gate still blank: «announced» is the moment a number appears, and «yet» waits at the end of the question like a passenger by the empty gate.

grammar.title: «Yet» and the present perfect
grammar.text: «Has… been announced yet?» asks whether something expected has happened by now. «Yet» goes at the end, and the verb is in the present perfect: «has been announced».

pronunciation.title: «Announced» ends in -nst
pronunciation.respelling: haz thuh GAYT bin uh-NOWNST yet
pronunciation.text: The ending of «announced» is a quick t after s: three sounds in a row, n, s, t, with no vowel added. Put the stress on the second syllable: a-NOUNCED.

phrases.target: Is this OK as hand luggage?

translations.bg-BG: Става ли това за ръчен багаж?

mnemonic.title: Luggage for your hand
mnemonic.text: It says what it is: luggage you carry in your hand. Your own language builds the same two-word name, so picture a small bag held at your side.

grammar.title: «As», not «like»
grammar.text: «As» says what something is used or counted as: «OK as hand luggage». «Like» means “similar to” and doesn't fit here. Many languages use one word for both.

pronunciation.title: A short u in «luggage»
pronunciation.respelling: iz this oh-KAY uz HAND lug-ij
pronunciation.text: The u in «luggage» is the short, relaxed vowel of «cup»: not a clear “a” and not “oo”. The ending is a quick ij, as in «village».

phrases.target: Is the flight to Paris on time?

translations.bg-BG: Навреме ли е полетът за Париж?

mnemonic.title: On the clock
mnemonic.text: Picture the plane parked right on the clock face at the planned minute: «on time» means exactly then. «In time» is a different phrase, for being early enough.

grammar.title: «On time» or «in time»
grammar.text: «On time» means at the planned moment: the flight leaves on time. «In time» means early enough for something: «We got there in time for the flight». Your own language may use one word for both.

pronunciation.title: «Paris» is stressed at the start
pronunciation.ipa: [ɪz ðə ˈflaɪt tə ˈpær.ɪs ɒn ˈtaɪm]
pronunciation.respelling: iz thuh FLITE tuh PA-riss on TIME
pronunciation.text: Stress the first syllable, PA-riss, and end on a plain s, not the zh-like ending the name has in your own language. The second vowel is short and weak.

mnemonic.title: A case for a suit
mnemonic.text: A «suitcase» is «suit» + «case»: a case for a suit of clothes. Picture one neat suit folded inside the bag that has not come round on the belt.

grammar.title: «Has» for one, «have» for more
grammar.text: The present perfect, «has/have» + past participle, links the past to now: the bag isn't here yet. One suitcase takes «hasn't»; several bags take «haven't»: «My bags haven't arrived».

pronunciation.title: «Arrived»: a voiced v
pronunciation.text: In «arrived» the ending is just a d after a voiced v: uh-RYVD, two syllables, no extra vowel. Don't let the v turn into f.

phrases.target: Could you give me a hand, please?

translations.bg-BG: Може ли да ми помогнете, моля?
translations.ru-RU: Вы не могли бы мне помочь, пожалуйста?

mnemonic.title: A hand that helps
mnemonic.text: A hand is help: picture someone holding out a hand to pull you up. Your own language has the same picture, so «give me a hand» is easy to guess.

grammar.title: «Could you…?» for a polite request
grammar.text: «Could you…?» is the polite way to ask for help. «Could» is followed by the bare verb: «give», never “to give”.

pronunciation.title: A soft h, a short a
pronunciation.ipa: [kʊd ju ˈɡɪv mi ə ˈhænd ˈpliːz]
pronunciation.respelling: kood yoo GIV mee uh HAND, PLEEZ
pronunciation.text: The h of «hand» is only a breath of air from the throat, much softer than a scraping “kh”. The vowel is short and open, as in «trap», not “e”.

phrases.target: Please call an ambulance. It's an emergency

translations.bg-BG: Моля, извикайте линейка. Спешен случай е
translations.ru-RU: Пожалуйста, вызовите скорую. Это очень срочно

mnemonic.title: Emergency comes from «emerge»
mnemonic.text: An «emergency» is something that suddenly emerges, comes out of nowhere. In Britain you dial 999 for an ambulance, and 112 works too.

grammar.title: Polite commands with «please»
grammar.text: A command is just the plain verb with no subject: «Call an ambulance». Put «please» at the start or the end to make it polite: «Please call…» or «Call…, please». The next sentence names the situation: «It's an emergency».

pronunciation.title: AM-byuh-lunss and ih-MUR-jen-see
pronunciation.ipa: [ˈpliːz ˈkɔːl ən ˈæm.bjʊ.ləns ɪts ən ɪˈmɜː.dʒən.si]
pronunciation.respelling: PLEEZ KAWL un AM-byuh-lunss, its un ih-MUR-jen-see
pronunciation.text: «Ambulance» is stressed on its first syllable: AM-byuh-lunss. In «emergency» the stress is on the second syllable, ih-MUR-jen-see: a long vowel as in «bird», no r sound, and the g is a j.

mnemonic.title: Steal, stole, stolen
mnemonic.text: Chant the three forms before you say the phrase: steal, stole, stolen. They all start with st, and the o of «stole» comes back in «stolen».

grammar.title: «Someone's» means «someone has»
grammar.text: The present perfect, «has» + past participle, gives recent news that still matters. Here «'s» is «has», not «is», because «stolen» is a participle.

pronunciation.title: The gliding o in «stolen»
pronunciation.text: The vowel in «stolen» is a glide: it starts at a weak “uh” and moves to “oo”, not a pure short “o”. Say STOH-lun slowly and let your lips round as you go.

mnemonic.title: Two old friends
mnemonic.text: Both words are in your own language too: the police and a station. Join them in your head as a station with a blue lamp over the door.

grammar.title: «Police station»: two nouns
grammar.text: In «police station» the first noun says what kind of station it is, and it takes no -s: «police station», «bus station», «train station». «Where's» is short for «where is».

pronunciation.title: po-LEESS: stress on -lice
pronunciation.text: Stress «police» on the second syllable, like the word in your own language: puh-LEESS, ending in s. The -tion of «station» is sh: STAY-shun.

phrases.target: I've lost my passport. What should I do?

translations.bg-BG: Изгубих паспорта си. Какво да правя?
translations.ru-RU: У меня пропал паспорт. Что мне делать?

mnemonic.title: Pass + port
mnemonic.text: A «passport» lets you pass through a port: «pass» + «port». It is the one document you must not lose.

grammar.title: «What should I do?»
grammar.text: «Should» gives or asks for advice, and it is followed by the bare verb: «What should I do?». It never takes «to» or an -s.

pronunciation.title: No r in «passport»
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪv ˈlɒst maɪ ˈpɑːs.pɔːt ˈwɒt ʃəd aɪ ˈduː]
pronunciation.respelling: ive LOST my PAHSS-pawt, WOT shood eye DOO
pronunciation.text: British English drops the r before a consonant: PAHSS-pawt, with a long open “ah” and a long “aw”. The stress is on the first syllable.

phrases.target: I've got a meeting at ten

mnemonic.title: A table, chairs and a clock
mnemonic.text: Picture a round table with chairs and a clock pointing to ten. A «meeting» is what happens when people «meet», with -ing added.

grammar.title: «I've got» means «I have»
grammar.text: British English often says «I've got» for «I have». It is present tense: «got» doesn't make it past. «At» goes with clock times: «at ten».

pronunciation.title: Long ee, short i
pronunciation.respelling: ive GOT uh MEE-ting at TEN
pronunciation.text: In «meeting» the first vowel is long: MEE-. The second is short and relaxed: -ting. Don't give both syllables the same vowel.

phrases.target: Could you send me the report by Friday?

translations.bg-BG: Може ли да ми изпратиш доклада до петък?
translations.ru-RU: Не могли бы вы прислать мне отчёт до пятницы?

mnemonic.title: A finish line on Friday
mnemonic.text: Picture a finish line drawn on Friday, with the report already across it. «By» means “no later than”.

grammar.title: «By» is not «until»
grammar.text: «By Friday» means on or before Friday: it is a deadline. «Until Friday» means all the way up to Friday and then stops. Your own language uses a single word for both.

pronunciation.title: A soft English r
pronunciation.ipa: [kʊd ju ˈsend mi ðə rɪˈpɔːt baɪ ˈfraɪ.deɪ]
pronunciation.respelling: kood yoo SEND mee thuh ri-PAWT by FRY-day
pronunciation.text: Make the r in «Friday» and «report» with the tongue curled back and not touching anything: no rolling. At the end of «report» there is no r at all, and the stress falls on -PORT.

phrases.target: I work from home on Fridays

translations.ru-RU: По пятницам я работаю из дома

mnemonic.title: A row of Fridays
mnemonic.text: Picture a row of Fridays on a calendar, with you on the sofa with a laptop in every one. The -s on «Fridays» means every Friday.

grammar.title: «On Fridays» means every Friday
grammar.text: A day name with -s describes a habit: «on Fridays» is every Friday, while «on Friday» is one particular Friday. Routines use the present simple: «I work».

pronunciation.title: No r in «work»
pronunciation.respelling: eye WERK frum HOHM on FRY-dayz
pronunciation.text: «Work» has no r sound: it is a long “er” as in «bird», then k. «From» is quick and weak, like “frum”.

mnemonic.title: Word for word
mnemonic.text: Word for word this is the question you already ask in your own language: have you a little minute? Picture a colleague tapping on your desk and holding up one finger.

grammar.title: Answer with «have»
grammar.text: Short answers repeat «have»: «Yes, I have» or «Sorry, I haven't». Don't answer «Yes, I got»: it sounds like the past.

pronunciation.title: MIN-it, not mi-NOOT
pronunciation.text: The noun «minute» has two short syllables, with the stress at the start: MIN-it. Don't copy the stress or the long u of the word in your own language.

phrases.target: I'll finish it by the end of the day

translations.bg-BG: Ще го довърша до края на деня

mnemonic.title: Sunset on the to-do list
mnemonic.text: Picture the sun going down with the last item on your list ticked. Word for word it matches your own language: «by the end of the day».

grammar.title: «I'll» for a promise
grammar.text: «I'll» (I will) is how you promise or offer something at work. It is followed by the bare verb: «I'll finish», never “I'll to finish”.

pronunciation.title: Short, weak little words
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪl ˈfɪn.ɪʃ ɪt baɪ ði ˈend əv ðə ˈdeɪ]
pronunciation.respelling: eyel FIN-ish it by thee END uv thuh DAY
pronunciation.text: «Finish», «end» and «day» carry the stress. «By», «of» and «the» are quick and weak: «of» is just “uv”, and «the» before a vowel is “thee”.

translations.bg-BG: Каква е паролата за уай-фай, моля?

mnemonic.title: A word that lets you pass
mnemonic.text: A «password» is «pass» + «word»: the word the doorkeeper wants before you may pass. Your own language borrowed it from French «parole», “word”, so the idea is the same.

grammar.title: Noun + noun: «Wi-Fi password»
grammar.text: In English the first noun describes the second, with no «of» or «for»: «Wi-Fi password», «phone charger», «bus ticket». The main noun comes last.

pronunciation.title: Stress on the first syllable
pronunciation.text: In «Wi-Fi» and «password» the stress is on the first syllable: WY-fy, PAHSS-werd. The first vowel of «password» is a long, open “ah”.

phrases.target: My phone's dying. Could I borrow your charger?

translations.bg-BG: Батерията ми почти свърши. Може ли да взема зарядното ви назаем?
translations.ru-RU: Телефон садится. Можно одолжить вашу зарядку?

mnemonic.title: A phone that «dies»
mnemonic.text: Your own language probably says a phone «dies» when the battery runs flat. Picture the red battery icon as a heartbeat line going flat.

grammar.title: «Borrow» is not «lend»
grammar.text: You «borrow» something from someone and give it back; they «lend» it to you. «Could I borrow your charger?» means the same as «Could you lend me your charger?». Your own language may use one verb for both.

pronunciation.title: Ch and j in «charger»
pronunciation.ipa: [maɪ ˈfəʊnz ˈdaɪ.ɪŋ kʊd aɪ ˈbɒr.əʊ jɔː ˈtʃɑː.dʒə]
pronunciation.respelling: my FOHNZ DY-ing, kood eye BOR-oh yaw CHAH-juh
pronunciation.text: «Charger» starts with ch, as in «church», and its g is a j. British English has no r at the end: CHAH-juh.

mnemonic.title: Make the phone ring
mnemonic.text: «To ring» means to make someone's phone ring. Your own language uses the same picture for a phone call, so imagine a screen lighting up with your name.

grammar.title: Ring someone, no «to»
grammar.text: British English says «ring someone» with no preposition: «ring you», never “ring to you”. «Ring» is the usual British word for phoning; «call» works too and is the American choice.

pronunciation.title: ng with no g
pronunciation.text: In «ring» the ng is one sound at the back of the mouth. Don't add a g or a k after it, and slide straight into «you».

phrases.target: I can't get any signal here

mnemonic.title: Empty bars
mnemonic.text: «Signal» is the same word you know from your own language. Picture the bars in the corner of your screen, all empty: not even one, and that is what «any» means here.

grammar.title: One negative is enough
grammar.text: In English one negative is enough: «can't get any signal», never “can't get no signal”. Languages with double negatives tempt learners to add a second one.

pronunciation.title: The g in «signal»
pronunciation.respelling: eye KAHNT get EN-ee SIG-nul HEER
pronunciation.text: In «signal» the g is pronounced: SIG-nul, with a short i. Compare «sign», where the g is silent and the vowel is long.

phrases.target: Could you text me the address?

translations.bg-BG: Можеш ли да ми пратиш адреса по есемес?

mnemonic.title: A text, then «text me»
mnemonic.text: A «text» is a short written message, and here the noun has become a verb: «text me» means “send me a text”. Picture a speech bubble flying to your phone with an address pin on it.

grammar.title: The person first, no «to»
grammar.text: With «text», «send» and «give», put the person first and drop «to»: «text me the address». If you use «to», the order flips: «text the address to me».

pronunciation.title: uh-DRESS: stress at the end
pronunciation.respelling: kood yoo TEKST mee thee uh-DRESS
pronunciation.text: Stress the second syllable of «address»: uh-DRESS. The first vowel is a weak “uh”, not a full “a”, unlike the word in your own language.

phrases.target: I've got a brother and a sister

translations.ru-RU: У меня есть брат и сестра

mnemonic.title: Old family words
mnemonic.text: «Brother» and «sister» are relatives of the words in your own language: you can hear the br-…-r in one and the s-…-str in the other. They come from the same ancestors.

grammar.title: «A» before each noun
grammar.text: A singular countable noun needs «a» (or «the», «my»): «a brother and a sister». Bulgarian and Russian speakers often leave it out, so repeat «a» before each noun.

pronunciation.title: A voiced th in «brother»
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪv ˈɡɒt ə ˈbrʌð.ər ən ə ˈsɪs.tə]
pronunciation.respelling: ive GOT uh BRUDH-er un uh SIS-tuh
pronunciation.text: The th in «brother» is voiced: put the tip of your tongue lightly between your teeth and let your voice buzz, as in «the». The vowel is the short “uh” of «cup».

mnemonic.title: A polite knock
mnemonic.text: Picture a polite knock at a door: «any» asks whether there are some at all, which is why it belongs in questions.

grammar.title: Child, children
grammar.text: The plural of «child» is «children», not “childs”: an irregular plural with no -s. Learn it together with man → men and person → people.

pronunciation.title: Two vowels: child and children
pronunciation.text: «Child» has the long “eye” sound, but «children» has a short i: CHIL-drun. Don't put a vowel between l and d.

phrases.target: My mum lives in a small town

translations.bg-BG: Майка ми живее в малък град
translations.ru-RU: Моя мама живёт в небольшом городе

mnemonic.title: The start of mama
mnemonic.text: «Mum» sounds like the first half of «mama»: both are built on the «m» that babies make early on. British children say «mum»; Americans say «mom».

grammar.title: -s after he, she and it
grammar.text: In the present simple only «he», «she» and «it» take -s: «my mum lives», but «I live» and «my parents live».

pronunciation.title: A long aw and a gliding ow
pronunciation.ipa: [maɪ ˈmʌm ˈlɪvz ɪn ə ˈsmɔːl ˈtaʊn]
pronunciation.respelling: my MUM LIVZ in uh SMAWL TOWN
pronunciation.text: «Small» has a long, rounded “aw”, not a short “o”. «Town» glides from “ah” to “oo”, as in «now», not «ton».

translations.bg-BG: Дъщеря ми е на пет години

mnemonic.title: Daughter rhymes with water
mnemonic.text: Picture her holding a glass: in British English «daughter» rhymes with «water», DAW-tuh and WAW-tuh. The gh is silent.

grammar.title: Age uses «be»
grammar.text: English gives age with «be»: «my daughter is five», «I'm thirty». «Years old» is optional, and «have» is never used.

pronunciation.title: A silent gh
pronunciation.text: The gh in «daughter» is silent, and the vowel is a long “aw”: DAW-tuh, with no r at the end.

phrases.target: We're visiting my grandparents on Sunday

translations.bg-BG: В неделя ще ходим при баба и дядо
translations.ru-RU: В воскресенье мы едем к бабушке и дедушке

mnemonic.title: Grand parents
mnemonic.text: «Grand» + «parents»: the parents of your parents. Picture a big family photo with two white-haired people in the middle.

grammar.title: The present continuous for a plan
grammar.text: For a plan that is already arranged, English uses the present continuous: «We're visiting… on Sunday», which sounds more natural than «We will visit». «On» goes with days.

pronunciation.title: W and v
pronunciation.respelling: weer VIZ-i-ting my GRAN-pair-unts on SUN-day
pronunciation.text: Make w with rounded lips and no teeth, and v with your top teeth on your lower lip: «we're» and «visiting» are a pair to practise. Stress «visiting» on the first syllable: VIZ-i-ting.

phrases.target: I'd like to book a table for four, please

translations.bg-BG: Може ли да запазя маса за четирима, моля?
translations.ru-RU: Можно забронировать столик на четверых, пожалуйста?

mnemonic.title: A name in the book
mnemonic.text: You «book» a table by writing it in a book: picture the restaurant's reservation book with your name on the page. The verb and the book are the same word.

grammar.title: «I'd like to» + verb
grammar.text: «I'd like» (I would like) is softer and more polite than «I want». After it comes «to» and the bare verb: «I'd like to book».

pronunciation.title: A short oo in «book»
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪd ˈlaɪk tə ˈbʊk ə ˈteɪ.bəl fə ˈfɔː ˈpliːz]
pronunciation.respelling: eyed LIKE tuh BOOK uh TAY-bul fuh FAW, PLEEZ
pronunciation.text: «Book» has a short, relaxed vowel, the same as in «good» and «look»: not the long “oo” of «boot». «Four» is long and has no r sound.

phrases.target: Do you have a table free at eight?

translations.bg-BG: Имате ли свободна маса в осем?
translations.ru-RU: У вас есть свободный столик на восемь?

mnemonic.title: A table is a flat board
mnemonic.text: «Table» comes from Latin «tabula», a flat board, which also gave Bulgarian and Russian «tablitsa», a table of figures. Picture a flat board laid for dinner, with a clock showing eight.

grammar.title: «At» for clock times
grammar.text: «At» goes with clock times: «at eight», «at half past seven». Days take «on» («on Friday») and months take «in» («in May»).

pronunciation.title: Two syllables in «table»
pronunciation.ipa: [də ju ˈhæv ə ˈteɪ.bəl ˈfriː ət ˈeɪt]
pronunciation.respelling: duh yoo HAV uh TAY-bul FREE at AYT
pronunciation.text: «Table» has two syllables, TAY-bul: the second has no real vowel, just a quick «b» and an «l» made with the tip of the tongue behind the top teeth. «Eight» is a long «ay» with a clear final t.

phrases.target: I've got a booking at seven, under Petrov

translations.bg-BG: Имам резервация за седем, на името на Петров
translations.ru-RU: У меня бронь на семь, на фамилию Петров

mnemonic.title: Filed under P
mnemonic.text: Picture the host running a finger down the page of the reservation book until it stops at the letter P. Your booking is filed «under» your surname.

grammar.title: «Under», not «on»
grammar.text: A booking is «under» a name: «under Petrov». Your own language uses a different preposition here, but English uses «under».

pronunciation.title: SEV-n: stress at the start
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪv ˈɡɒt ə ˈbʊk.ɪŋ ət ˈsev.ən ˈʌn.də ˈpet.rɒv]
pronunciation.respelling: ive GOT uh BOOK-ing at SEV-n, UN-duh PET-rov
pronunciation.text: Stress the first syllable of «seven»: SEV-n, with the second syllable nearly gone. Don't put the stress on the end.

mnemonic.title: Booking essential
mnemonic.text: Picture the sign on a busy restaurant door: “Booking essential”. Your question is the polite version of that sign.

grammar.title: «Do we need to…?»
grammar.text: In everyday speech «need» is an ordinary verb, so the question takes «do»: «Do we need to…?». The next verb follows «to» in its bare form: «to book».

pronunciation.title: Long ee, voiced d
pronunciation.text: «Need» has a long “ee” and ends in a voiced d, not a t: keep it long and clear before «to»: NEED tuh BOOK.

phrases.target: Sorry, I need to cancel our booking for tonight

translations.bg-BG: Съжалявам, трябва да отменя резервацията ни за довечера
translations.ru-RU: Извините, мне нужно отменить нашу бронь на сегодня

mnemonic.title: Crossed out with an X
mnemonic.text: To «cancel» is to cross a name out of the book with a big X. Picture the waiter doing that to your table.

grammar.title: «For tonight»
grammar.text: A booking is «for» a time: «for tonight», «for Friday», «for seven». «Tonight» takes no preposition of its own, so never “in tonight”.

pronunciation.title: CAN-sul and tuh-NITE
pronunciation.ipa: [ˈsɒr.i aɪ ˈniːd tə ˈkæn.səl ˈaʊə ˈbʊk.ɪŋ fə təˈnaɪt]
pronunciation.respelling: SOR-ee eye NEED tuh CAN-sul OW-uh BOOK-ing fuh tuh-NITE
pronunciation.text: «Cancel» is stressed at the start: CAN-sul, with the short open “a” of «cat». «Tonight» goes the other way: tuh-NITE, with a weak first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Аптека: the apothecary's shop
mnemonic.text: «Аптека» comes from the same Greek word as English “apothecary”, meaning “storehouse”: the shop where remedies are kept.

grammar.title: Adjectives match the noun
grammar.text: «Аптека» is feminine, so the adjective ends in «-ая»: «ближайшая аптека». Russian has no “the” or “a”, and no word for “is” in the present tense.

pronunciation.title: Gde zdes: no vowel in between
pronunciation.text: «Где здесь» has two consonant clusters, «гд» and «зд»: say them without a vowel in between. «Ближайшая» is stressed on «-жай-», and the ending «-шая» shrinks to a quick “shuh-yuh”.

phrases.target: У вас есть что-нибудь от головной боли?

translations.en-GB: Do you have anything for a headache?

mnemonic.title: Головная боль: head pain
mnemonic.text: «Головная боль» is built like “headache”: «голова» (head) plus «боль» (pain). The root of «боль» also gives «болит» (it hurts).

grammar.title: «От» + genitive for remedies
grammar.text: «От» plus the genitive says what a remedy is for: «от головной боли», «от кашля» (for a cough). «Что-нибудь» is “anything”, and «У вас есть…?» is how Russian asks “do you have…?”, literally “at you is…?”.

pronunciation.title: Weak о before the stress
pronunciation.ipa: [u ˈvas ˈjesʲtʲ ˈʂto nʲɪˌbutʲ ɐd ɡəlɐvˈnoj ˈbolʲɪ]
pronunciation.respelling: oo VAHS YEST' SHTO nee-boot' uhd guh-luhv-NOY BO-lee
pronunciation.text: In «головной» the stress is on the last syllable, «-ной», so both earlier «о» shrink to weak vowels: guh-luhv-NOY. Before a voiced «г», the «т» of «от» is said as «д»: «ад головной».

mnemonic.title: Горло and gargle
mnemonic.text: «Горло» (throat) sounds a little like “gargle”, which is just what you do with it when it is sore.

grammar.title: The sore part is the subject
grammar.text: In «У меня болит…» (literally “at me hurts…”) the sore part is the subject, so the verb agrees with it: «болит горло» for one thing, «болят уши» for several.

pronunciation.title: Stress on -лит
pronunciation.text: The stress is on the last syllable of «болит», so the first «о» is weak, a short “buh”. The «л» is soft before «и»: lift the middle of the tongue, buh-LEET.

translations.en-GB: I need to see a doctor

mnemonic.title: To me, needed, to the doctor
mnemonic.text: Say it as a tiny story: «мне» (to me), «нужно» (needed), «к врачу» (to the doctor). That is how Russian “needs” things: the person is “to me”, not “I”.

grammar.title: «К» + dative
grammar.text: «К» means “to (a person)” and takes the dative: «врач» becomes «к врачу». The verb “go” is left out: «Мне нужно к врачу» is “I need [to go] to the doctor”.

pronunciation.title: Soft ч, stress on -чу
pronunciation.text: «Ч» is always soft: like the “ch” of “cheese” with the tongue flat and forward. The stress is on the last syllable, so the «а» before it is weak: vruh-CHOO.

mnemonic.title: Allergy in Cyrillic
mnemonic.text: «Аллергия» is “allergy” written in Cyrillic, with «лл» for ll and the ending «-ия» you also see in «история» and «география». «Орехи» are nuts.

grammar.title: Allergy «на» + accusative
grammar.text: Russian says “allergy on” something: «аллергия на» plus the accusative, here «орехи». «У меня…» (“at me [is]…”) is the usual way to say “I have”.

pronunciation.title: Weak о, rough х
pronunciation.text: In «орехи» the stress is on «-ре-», so the first «о» is a weak “uh”. The «х» is a rough “kh”, like Scottish “loch”, a little softer before «и». «Аллергия» has one stress, on «-ги-».

phrases.target: У меня бронь на фамилию Иванов

translations.en-GB: I've got a booking under the name Ivanov
translations.bg-BG: Имам резервация на името на Иванов

mnemonic.title: Бронь: the booking
mnemonic.text: On any hotel website you will see «бронирование» (booking) and a button «Забронировать»: «бронь» is the short spoken form of that same family.

grammar.title: «На» + accusative: under a name
grammar.text: «На» plus the accusative gives “in the name of”: «фамилия» (surname) becomes «фамилию». The surname itself stays unchanged: «на фамилию Иванов».

pronunciation.title: Иванов ends in an f
pronunciation.respelling: oo mee-NYA BRON' nuh fuh-MEE-lee-yoo ee-vuh-NOF
pronunciation.text: Many surnames in «-ов» (Иванов, Петров, Смирнов) are stressed on the last syllable, and the final «в» is said as «ф»: a voiced consonant at the end of a word turns voiceless.

mnemonic.title: One chant for the meals
mnemonic.text: Learn the three meals as one chant: «завтрак, обед, ужин» (breakfast, lunch, dinner). Note that «обед» is lunch, the main midday meal.

grammar.title: «Во сколько?»: at what time
grammar.text: «Во сколько…?» is the standard way to ask “at what time…?”: «в» (“at”) becomes «во» before a tight group of consonants such as «ск». There is no verb in the present tense: «Во сколько завтрак?» is literally “At how-much breakfast?”.

pronunciation.title: «В» sounds like ф in завтрак
pronunciation.text: In «завтрак» the «в» is said as «ф» because it sits before the voiceless «т»: ZAF-truhk, never “zav”. The last «а» is weak, a short “uh”.

translations.en-GB: Could you bring another towel, please?
translations.bg-BG: Донесете ми още една кърпа, моля

mnemonic.title: Полотенце: a small piece of cloth
mnemonic.text: «Полотенце» grows out of «полотно» (linen cloth, canvas), so a towel is a small piece of cloth.

grammar.title: «Пожалуйста» after the verb
grammar.text: «Принесите, пожалуйста, …» is the usual order for a polite request: «пожалуйста» sits right after the verb, between commas. «Одно» is neuter to match «полотенце», and a neuter noun looks the same as an object as in its basic form, so «ещё одно полотенце» does not change.

pronunciation.title: Щ is a long soft sh
pronunciation.text: «Щ» is a long, soft «ш»: often approximated as the “sh-ch” of “fresh cheese”, but said as one sound with the tongue flat and forward. «Ещё» is yee-SHCHO, and «ё» is always stressed.

translations.en-GB: There's no hot water in the room

mnemonic.title: Горячая вода: water that burns
mnemonic.text: «Горячий» (hot) shares its root with «гореть» (to burn): hot water is water that “burns”. You will meet «горячая вода» (“hot water”) on notices and utility bills.

grammar.title: «Нет» takes the genitive
grammar.text: After «нет» (there is no) comes the genitive: «вода» becomes «воды» and «горячая» becomes «горячей». Absence changes the endings. «Номер» here is the hotel room, not a number.

pronunciation.title: The vowel ы
pronunciation.text: «Ы» (“uy” in the respelling) is the hard partner of «и»: say “ee” with the tongue pulled back and flat. «Воды» ends in it, with the stress on the last syllable: vuh-DUY.

translations.en-GB: Can I leave my suitcase until this evening?
translations.bg-BG: Може ли да оставя куфара си до вечерта?

mnemonic.title: Чемо-ДАН: Dan's suitcase
mnemonic.text: The stress of «чемодан» falls on the last syllable, «-дан»: picture a man called Dan hauling a suitcase, «чемо-Дан».

grammar.title: «Можно» + infinitive
grammar.text: «Можно» plus an infinitive asks permission, and no “I” is needed: «Можно оставить…?» is “May I leave…?”. «До» means “until” and takes the genitive: «вечер» becomes «до вечера».

pronunciation.title: Weak vowels, strong -дан
pronunciation.text: Only «-дан» carries the stress, so the «е» and «о» before it are weak: chee-muh-DAN. The «ч» is soft, as always.

phrases.target: У вас есть это в другом размере?

translations.en-GB: Do you have this in another size?
translations.bg-BG: Имате ли това в друг размер?

mnemonic.title: At you, is there…?
mnemonic.text: Hear «у вас есть» as a little picture: you point at the shop assistant, “at you, is there…?”. The same three words open nearly every “Do you have…?”.

grammar.title: «В» + prepositional
grammar.text: «В» (in) with a state or place takes the prepositional case: «размер» becomes «в размере» and «другой» becomes «в другом». Masculine endings: «-е» on the noun, «-ом» on the adjective.

pronunciation.title: Final unstressed е is “i”
pronunciation.ipa: [u ˈvas ˈjesʲtʲ ˈɛtə v druˈɡom rɐzˈmʲerʲɪ]
pronunciation.respelling: oo VAHS YEST' E-tuh v droo-GOM ruz-MYEH-ree
pronunciation.text: An unstressed «е» at the end of a word is a short “i”, not “eh”: «размере» ends in “-ree”. The stress is on «-ме-», and on the last syllable of «другом»: droo-GOM.

mnemonic.title: Measure it on
mnemonic.text: «Примерить» is «при-» (on, up against) plus «мерить» (to measure): trying something on is measuring it against yourself.

grammar.title: Perfective: one try-on
grammar.text: «Примерить» is perfective: a single try-on that gets finished. Its imperfective twin «примерять» describes trying things on over and over. After «можно», use the perfective when you ask for one go.

pronunciation.title: Soft ть, stress on -ме-
pronunciation.text: The final «ть» is a soft «т»: lift the middle of the tongue as if adding a faint “y”. The stress is on «-ме-»: pree-MYEH-reet'.

mnemonic.title: Нибудь: “be it anything”
mnemonic.text: «-нибудь» ends in «будь», the command “be”: «что-нибудь» is “whatever it may be”, so “anything”. It even sounds like “boot”: picture a boot with a price tag and ask for anything cheaper.

grammar.title: по- + the comparative
grammar.text: «Дешевле» (cheaper) is the comparative of «дешёвый» (cheap) and never changes its ending. The prefix «по-» softens it: «подешевле» is “a bit cheaper”, a polite way to ask.

pronunciation.title: Ш is always hard
pronunciation.text: «Ш» is always hard, even before «е»: say “sheh”, never “shyeh”. The stress is on «-ше-»: puh-dee-SHEV-lee.

translations.en-GB: It's a bit big on me

mnemonic.title: Велико: too great for you
mnemonic.text: «Велик» is the word in «великий» (great). Said of clothes it means “too big”: the garment is “too great” for you. Learn the pair «велико» (too big) and «мало» (too small).

grammar.title: Short adjectives mean “too…”
grammar.text: Short forms such as «велик, велика, велико, велики» mean “too big for me” and agree with the thing: «это» is neuter, so «велико». The person it does not fit goes in the dative: «мне». For a skirt: «Юбка мне велика».

pronunciation.title: Stress on the last syllable
pronunciation.text: «Велико» is stressed on «-ко», so the first two vowels are weak: vee-lee-KO. The «л» is soft before «и». Compare «великий» (great), stressed on «-ли-».

mnemonic.title: «Смотрю»: a viewing platform
mnemonic.text: «Смотрю» is “I look”, from the same root as «смотровая площадка», a viewing platform: a place you go only to look. «Просто» means “just”, so «Я просто смотрю» says you are only browsing.

grammar.title: One present tense
grammar.text: Russian has a single present tense for “I look” and “I'm looking”: «я смотрю». The ending «-ю» goes with «я» (I), as in «я работаю».

pronunciation.title: Stress on -рю
pronunciation.text: The stress is on the last syllable of «смотрю», so the first «о» is weak: smuh-TRYOO. The «р» is tapped, and soft before «ю».

mnemonic.title: Занято: busy with
mnemonic.text: «Заниматься» (to be busy with, to do) is built on «занят» (busy): the sign «Занято» on a toilet door means “occupied”. What you do is what you are busy with.

grammar.title: «Заниматься» + instrumental
grammar.text: «Заниматься» takes the instrumental case with no preposition: «чем?» (with what?) is the instrumental of «что». The answer uses it too: «Я занимаюсь спортом» (I do sport).

pronunciation.title: Stress on -ма-
pronunciation.text: «Занимаетесь» has five syllables, and the stress is on the third, «-ма-»: zuh-nee-MA-yih-tyihs'. The vowels around it are weak, and the final «сь» is soft.

mnemonic.title: Ты is “thou”
mnemonic.text: «Ты» is the Russian “thou”: the two share an ancient root, and like “thou” it is for friends, family and children, while «вы» is the polite “you”.

grammar.title: «Давайте»: let's
grammar.text: «Давайте» (the polite or plural form of «давай», “come on, let's”) starts a suggestion; here the verb is left out. After «на», «ты» and «вы» do not change: «на ты» (informal), «на вы» (formal).

pronunciation.title: «Ты» is not «ти»
pronunciation.text: The vowel in «ты» is «ы», a hard “i” made with the tongue pulled back. Compare «ти» ([tʲi], soft) with «ты» ([tɨ], hard): the letter decides the sound.

mnemonic.title: Язык: tongue and language
mnemonic.text: «Язык» means both “tongue” and “language”, just as English says “mother tongue”: you are learning the Russian tongue.

grammar.title: «Учить» takes an object
grammar.text: «Учить» (to learn, to study) takes a direct object: «Я учу русский язык». A masculine thing without a soul looks the same in the accusative, so «русский язык» does not change. Do not mix it up with «учиться» (to study as a student), which takes no direct object.

pronunciation.title: Doubled с, weak я
pronunciation.text: The doubled «сс» in «русский» is held a touch longer: ROOS-skee. The stress in «язык» is on the last syllable, so «я» turns into a weak “yi”: yih-ZUYK.

mnemonic.title: Жив-: alive
mnemonic.text: «Живёте» contains «жив-», “alive”, a distant cousin of the «viv-» in “vivid” and “survive”. To live is to be alive: «жить», «живой», «жизнь».

grammar.title: Present for what continues
grammar.text: Russian uses the present tense for something that began in the past and goes on: «Вы давно здесь живёте?» is “Have you lived here long?”. «Давно» means “for a long time”.

pronunciation.title: Жи sounds like zhih
pronunciation.text: After «ж» (and «ш», «ц») the letter «и» is pronounced «ы»: «жи» is “zhuy”, not “zhee”. «Ё» is always stressed: zhuy-VYO-tee.

mnemonic.title: по- … -ски: any language
mnemonic.text: Here is one recipe for any language: «по-» in front and «-ски» at the end. So «по-английски», «по-русски», «по-болгарски».

grammar.title: «По-…-ски» after говорить
grammar.text: After «говорить», a language is an adverb, «по-английски», not an adjective: «говорить по-русски». «Вы говорите» uses the polite «вы» with the ending «-ите».

pronunciation.title: Weak о before the stress
pronunciation.text: «Говорите» is stressed on «-ри-», so both «о» are weak: guh-vuh-REE-tee. In «английски» the stress is on «-лий-»: uhn-GLEE-skee, with a hard «г» as in “go”.

mnemonic.title: Погода: a pagoda in the rain
mnemonic.text: «Погода» sounds like “pagoda”: picture a pagoda in the rain, and “weather” will follow.

grammar.title: «Какая» agrees with «погода»
grammar.text: «Какая» is the feminine form of «какой» (what kind of) because «погода» is feminine, like most nouns ending in «-а». The masculine is «какой» and the neuter «какое».

pronunciation.title: Сегодня is said sevodnya
pronunciation.text: In «сегодня» the «г» is pronounced «в»: see-VOD-nya. The same happens in the endings «-ого» and «-его».

mnemonic.title: Жара: the family of жарить
mnemonic.text: «Жара» (heat) is in the family of «жарить» (to fry, to roast): heat so strong you could fry an egg.

grammar.title: «Ну и…» + noun
grammar.text: «Ну и» plus a noun makes an exclamation, “what a…”: «Ну и жара», «Ну и погода», «Ну и день». There is no verb.

pronunciation.title: Hard ж, stress on the end
pronunciation.text: «Жара» is stressed on the last syllable, so the first «а» is weak: zhuh-RA. The «ж» is always hard, like the “s” in “measure”.

translations.en-GB: Is it going to rain tomorrow?

mnemonic.title: Дождь: “dosh” from the sky
mnemonic.text: Hear «дождь» as “dosht”, close to British “dosh” (money): picture money pouring down tomorrow.

grammar.title: «Будет» + noun: “there will be”
grammar.text: Russian has no “it” for weather: «будет дождь» is “there will be rain”, with «дождь» as the subject. «Будет» is the future of «быть» (to be). A yes/no question is just rising intonation: «Завтра будет дождь?».

pronunciation.title: Дождь is said dosht
pronunciation.text: «Дождь» is written with «жд» but said “dosht'”: the voiced «жд» turns into voiceless «шт», and the soft sign leaves a light “y” at the end.

mnemonic.title: Зонтик: a sun-cover
mnemonic.text: «Зонтик» comes from Dutch zondek, “sun cover” (zon is “sun”, as in German Sonne): a sunshade that learned to handle rain.

grammar.title: «С собой»: with yourself
grammar.text: «Возьми» is the informal command of «взять» (to take); to a stranger or a group it is «возьмите». «С собой» means “with oneself” and never changes, whoever is taking the umbrella.

pronunciation.title: The soft sign in возьми
pronunciation.text: The soft sign «ь» in «возьми» makes the «з» soft before «м»: add a light “y” to the «з». The stress is on the last syllable: vuz'-MEE.

mnemonic.title: Холодно echoes “cold”
mnemonic.text: «Холодно» has the same consonant skeleton as English “cold”: х-л-д against c-l-d, in the same order. A chilly word for a chilly day.

grammar.title: No “it is” for temperature
grammar.text: Russian weather uses an adverb with no subject: «холодно» (cold), «жарко» (hot), «тепло» (warm). «На улице» (literally “on the street”) means “outside”.

pronunciation.title: Rough х, weak о
pronunciation.text: Only the first syllable is stressed in «холодно»: KHO-luhd-nuh. The «х» is a rough “kh”, like Scottish “loch”, never an English “h”, and the unstressed «о» shrinks to “uh”.

translations.en-GB: What are you up to tomorrow evening?

mnemonic.title: Делать: do a deal
mnemonic.text: Hear «дело» (a matter, business) as “deal”: «делать» is the verb for doing things, even “doing a deal”. «Делаешь» is “you do”.

grammar.title: Present for planned future
grammar.text: Russian often uses the present tense for plans: «Что ты делаешь завтра?» is “What are you doing tomorrow?”. «Вечером» (in the evening) is the instrumental and needs no preposition.

pronunciation.title: Что is said shto
pronunciation.text: «Что» is written with «чт» but said “shto”, never “chto”. In «вечером» the stress is on «ве-» and the ending «-ером» is weak: VYEH-chee-ruhm.

translations.bg-BG: Удобно ли ти е в седем?

mnemonic.title: Удобно hides доб-
mnemonic.text: «Удобно» hides «доб-», as in «добрый» (kind, good) and «Доброе утро»: something convenient is good for you.

grammar.title: Dative + удобно
grammar.text: The person goes in the dative, followed by an adverb, with no verb: «Тебе удобно?» (“to you [is it] convenient?”), «Мне удобно». The time is «в семь», with no «часов» needed.

pronunciation.title: «В семь» sounds like fsem
pronunciation.text: Before the voiceless «с», the preposition «в» is said as «ф»: [f sʲemʲ], almost one word, “fsyem”. The final «ь» keeps the «м» soft.

mnemonic.title: Давай: give it a go
mnemonic.text: «Давай» literally means “give”, but Russians use it as “come on, let's”. Think “give it a go”: «Давай встретимся» is “let's give meeting a go”.

grammar.title: Давай + we-form
grammar.text: «Давай» plus the «мы» form of a perfective verb means “let's…”: «встретимся» (we'll meet), «пойдём» (let's go). The ending «-ся» makes it mutual: “meet each other”.

pronunciation.title: Four consonants: встр
pronunciation.text: «Встретимся» opens with four consonants, [fstrʲ]: the «в» is said as «ф», and you do not add a vowel. The stress is on «-стре-», and the ending «-мся» is “msya”.

translations.en-GB: I'm running a bit late, sorry

mnemonic.title: Позд- hides in опаздываю
mnemonic.text: Spot the consonants п-з-д of «поздно» (late) inside «опаздываю»: that is the chunk for “late”.

grammar.title: Imperfective: running late
grammar.text: «Опаздываю» is imperfective, so it says you are late right now, in progress. The perfective «опоздаю» looks ahead (“I'll be late”). «Извини» is the informal sorry; to a stranger, say «извините».

pronunciation.title: Stress on -паз-, hard ы
pronunciation.text: Put the stress on «-паз-»: the first «о» becomes a weak “uh”. The «ы» in «-ды-» is the hard “i”, with the tongue pulled back: uh-PAZ-duy-vuh-yoo.

phrases.target: Сегодня не получится, может, в другой раз?

translations.en-GB: Today won't work. Maybe another time?
translations.bg-BG: Днес няма да стане, може би друг път?

mnemonic.title: Получится: it gets itself done
mnemonic.text: «Получится» is «получить» (to get) plus «-ся» (itself): in Russian, things “get themselves done”, they “work out”.

grammar.title: Perfective verbs point to the future
grammar.text: A perfective verb has no present tense: its present-looking form means the future. So «получится» is “it will work out” and «не получится» is “it won't”. «Может» (maybe) opens a soft suggestion.

pronunciation.title: -тся is said ц
pronunciation.ipa: [sʲɪˈvodnʲə nʲɪ pɐˈlut͡ɕɪt͡sə ˈmoʐɨt v druˈɡoj ˈras]
pronunciation.respelling: see-VOD-nya nee puh-LOO-chee-tsuh MO-zhuyt v droo-GOY RAS
pronunciation.text: «-тся» is pronounced “ts”: «получится» ends in “-chee-tsuh”, with one «ц», not “t-sya”. The stress is on «-лу-».

mnemonic.title: «Стойка»: where you stand
mnemonic.text: «Регистрация» is “registration”, the word you know from every airport. «Стойка» is a counter, and it hides «стоять» (“to stand”): you stand at it to check in.

grammar.title: The second noun takes the genitive
grammar.text: Where English says “of”, Russian changes the ending of the second noun: «регистрация» becomes «регистрации» in «стойка регистрации» (“desk of check-in”). There is no word for “is” in the present tense, so «Где…?» is enough.

pronunciation.title: Stress on стра, and ци is “tsih”
pronunciation.text: Put the stress on «стра» (ree-gee-STRAH-tsih-ee) and let the other syllables shrink. After «ц» the letter «и» is spoken as «ы», a flat «i», so «ци» is “tsih”, not “tsee”.

translations.en-GB: Which gate do we board from?
translations.bg-BG: От кой изход се качваме на самолета?

mnemonic.title: Exit to the plane
mnemonic.text: «Выход» is an exit, so a gate is the way out to the plane. «Посадка» comes from «садиться» (“to sit down”): boarding is when you go and take your seat.

grammar.title: «С» + genitive means “from”
grammar.text: «С» followed by the genitive means “from”. That is why «выход» becomes «выхода» and «какой» becomes «какого».

pronunciation.title: г is said в, д is said т
pronunciation.text: In «какого» the «г» is pronounced «в»: kuh-KO-vuh. In «посадка» the «д» before «к» sounds like «т»: puh-SAT-kuh.

mnemonic.title: «Ручная» comes from «рука»
mnemonic.text: «Ручная» comes from «рука» (“hand”), so «ручная кладь» is “hand baggage”, the bag you carry yourself. Picture a hand gripping a small case.

grammar.title: «У меня»: “I have”
grammar.text: Everyday Russian does not use a verb “to have”: it says “at me” («у меня») and then the thing. «Есть» (“there is”) is left out when you say exactly what you have, as here.

pronunciation.title: Stress on -ня and -на
pronunciation.text: In «меня» the stress is on «я», so the «е» before it shrinks to a short «и»: mi-NYA. «Ручная» is stressed on «на», and the «ч» is always soft.

translations.en-GB: Could I have a window seat, please?
translations.bg-BG: Може ли място до прозореца, моля?

mnemonic.title: Window: the eye of the house
mnemonic.text: «Окно» (window) comes from «око», an old word for “eye”: a window is the eye of the house. Say «у окна» and picture an eye looking out.

grammar.title: «Можно» + a noun
grammar.text: «Можно» means “is it possible / may I”. Put a noun straight after it and it asks for that thing: «Можно место?» is “May I have a seat?”. After «у» (“by”) the noun takes the genitive: «окно» becomes «окна».

pronunciation.title: Hard ж, quick пожалуйста
pronunciation.text: «Ж» is always hard, like the s in “measure”, in both «можно» and «пожалуйста». In «пожалуйста» the stress is on «жа», the «й» is barely heard, and the last two vowels are weak: puh-ZHAH-luh-stuh.

mnemonic.title: A suitcase that did not fly in
mnemonic.text: «Прилетел» is «при-» (arriving) plus «лететь» (“to fly”): it “flew in”. A suitcase that «не прилетел» never made the trip.

grammar.title: при-, у-, вы-: where it goes
grammar.text: Prefixes on «лететь» (“to fly”) show direction: «прилететь» is to arrive by air, «улететь» to fly away, «вылететь» to depart. Learn them as pairs: «прилетел» (arrived) and «улетел» (left).

pronunciation.title: Stress at the end, vowels weaken
pronunciation.text: Both long words are stressed on the last syllable: «чемодан» is chee-muh-DAN and «прилетел» is pree-lee-TYEL. The unstressed vowels shrink, so the first «е» and «о» of «чемодан» sound like a short “i” and “uh”.

phrases.target: Вы не могли бы мне помочь?

translations.bg-BG: Бихте ли могли да ми помогнете?

mnemonic.title: Help is built on «мочь»
mnemonic.text: «Помочь» (“to help”) is built on «мочь» (“can, to be able”), the root you also hear in «могли». Helping is lending someone your ability.

grammar.title: Softening with «не… бы»
grammar.text: A negative question with «бы» is the polite way to ask: «Вы не могли бы…?» is “Couldn't you…?”. «Могли» is a past form, and adding «бы» turns it into “could”.

pronunciation.title: Flat ы and the stress on ли
pronunciation.respelling: VUY nee muh-GLEE buy mnee puh-MOCH
pronunciation.text: «Ы» is a flat, back “i”, said with the tongue pulled back and the lips unrounded: «вы» is “vuy”, not “vee”. In «могли» the stress is on «ли», so the first «о» weakens to «а»: muh-GLEE.

mnemonic.title: «Скорая»: the quick one
mnemonic.text: «Скорая помощь» is “quick help”: the ambulance. People shorten it to «скорая», so you only need to remember the “quick” one.

grammar.title: Accusative: -ая becomes -ую
grammar.text: The thing you call is the object, so it takes the accusative. Feminine adjectives in -ая change to -ую: «скорая» becomes «скорую». The ending -ите makes the command polite (to «вы»).

pronunciation.title: Stress on the first syllable
pronunciation.text: «Вызовите» and «скорую» are both stressed on the first syllable: VUY-zuh-vee-tee, SKO-roo-yoo. The «о» inside «вызовите» is unstressed and weakens to a short «а».

mnemonic.title: The thief's root: «кра-»
mnemonic.text: «Телефон» is the word you already know. The new part is «украли», from «красть» (“to steal”), which also gives «кража» (“theft”).

grammar.title: No subject: “they stole”
grammar.text: «Украли» is a plural past form with no «они» (“they”). Russian uses it when the thief is unknown, where English says “was stolen”: «у меня украли телефон», literally “at me they stole a phone”.

pronunciation.title: Soft л, and the stress at the end
pronunciation.text: Stress «кра» in «украли» and «фон» in «телефон», not the first syllable as in English. The «л» before «и» is soft, like the l in “leaf”, not the heavy l of “full”.

translations.en-GB: Where is the nearest police station?

mnemonic.title: «Ближайшее»: the nearest
mnemonic.text: «Ближайшее» is built on «близко» (“near”), and «полиция» sounds almost like “police”. Together: “where [is the] nearest section of police?”

grammar.title: The adjective copies the noun
grammar.text: «Отделение» is a neuter noun, so the adjective ends in -ее: «ближайшее». For a masculine noun it would be «ближайший», for a feminine one «ближайшая». «Полиции» (“of police”) is the genitive.

pronunciation.title: Three stresses in a long phrase
pronunciation.text: Say the stressed syllables clearly («жай», «ле», «ли») and let the rest shrink. The «ж» and «ш» are always hard, and «ше» after them sounds like «шы».

mnemonic.title: «Кто» + «нибудь»: anybody
mnemonic.text: «Кто-нибудь» is “anybody”: «кто» (“who”) plus «нибудь», the same ending as in «что-нибудь» (“anything”). Picture yourself calling it across a crowded hall, then adding the language.

grammar.title: «-нибудь» for questions
grammar.text: Add «-нибудь» to «кто» to ask about “anyone at all” when you do not know whether there is such a person. «Кто-то» is “somebody”, a particular person you know exists.

pronunciation.title: Final soft т, stress at the end
pronunciation.text: In «кто-нибудь» the main stress is on «кто», but «буд» keeps a light second stress, and the final «дь» is said as a soft «т»: nee-boot'. «Говорит» is stressed on the end: guh-vuh-REET.

translations.en-GB: I work from home on Fridays

mnemonic.title: Работа and “robot”
mnemonic.text: «Работаю» (“I work”) comes from «работа» (“work”), the same Slavic root that gave the world “robot”, from Czech “robota”. «Удалённо» is “remotely”: it comes from «даль», “distance”.

grammar.title: «По пятницам»: every Friday
grammar.text: «По» + a plural day in the dative means “on those days, regularly”: «по пятницам» is “on Fridays” in general. For one particular Friday you would say «в пятницу».

pronunciation.title: ё is always stressed
pronunciation.text: The letter «ё» is always stressed: «удалённо» is oo-duh-LYO-nuh. In «работаю» the stress is on «бо» (ruh-BO-tuh-yoo), and the other «а» and «о» weaken.

translations.en-GB: Can you send me the report?
translations.bg-BG: Можеш ли да ми изпратиш отчета?

mnemonic.title: «Прислать»: send it here
mnemonic.text: «Прислать» is «при-» (“towards me”) plus «слать» (“to send”), the root of «посылка» (“parcel”). Picture the report coming towards you.

grammar.title: Perfective for one request
grammar.text: «Прислать» is perfective: it asks for one sending that will be completed. The imperfective «присылать» would mean sending regularly. After «можешь», a one-off request uses the perfective.

pronunciation.title: Soft ть, and тч run together
pronunciation.text: The final «ть» in «прислать» is a soft «т»: pree-SLAT'. In «отчёт» the «т» and «ч» run together and the «ё» is stressed: uht-CHOT.

translations.en-GB: I'll be about ten minutes late

mnemonic.title: Number after the noun: a shrug
mnemonic.text: Hear «минут на десять» as a shrug in words: when «десять» trails behind «минут», the speaker means “ten, give or take”. «Минут» is “minutes”, the word you already know.

grammar.title: Number after the noun: about
grammar.text: Put the number after the noun and it becomes approximate: «минут на десять» is “about ten minutes”. The exact version is «на десять минут». «Опоздаю» is perfective, so it already means “I will be late”.

pronunciation.title: ZDA stress, soft ть
pronunciation.text: In «опоздаю» the stress is on «зда», and the first two «о» weaken to short «а»: uh-puh-ZDAH-yoo. «Десять» is stressed on «де» and ends in a soft «ть».

translations.en-GB: Could we move the meeting to tomorrow?
translations.bg-BG: Може ли да преместим срещата за утре?

mnemonic.title: «Пере-» + «нести»: carry across
mnemonic.text: «Перенести» is «пере-» (“across”) plus «нести» (“to carry”): you pick the meeting up and carry it across to tomorrow.

grammar.title: Feminine -а becomes -у
grammar.text: A feminine noun in -а changes to -у when it is the object: «встреча» (meeting) becomes «встречу». «На» + accusative then names the new time: «на завтра», «на пятницу».

pronunciation.title: в sounds like ф
pronunciation.text: Before a voiceless «с» the «в» is pronounced «ф»: «встречу» is FSTRYE-choo. In «завтра» the «в» also becomes «ф»: ZAF-tra. Say the clusters without adding a vowel.

mnemonic.title: A minute between two fingers
mnemonic.text: Picture a colleague at your desk holding up a thumb and finger, a pinch of time: «минутка» is a very small minute.

grammar.title: The friendly ending -ка
grammar.text: The suffix «-ка» makes a feminine noun small and friendly: «минута» becomes «минутка». It softens a request: you are asking for a tiny favour.

pronunciation.title: «Есть» starts with y
pronunciation.text: «Есть» starts with a “y” sound (YEST') and ends in a soft «ть». In «тебя» the stress is on «я», so the first «е» shrinks to «и»: tee-BYA.

mnemonic.title: Пароль is “parole”
mnemonic.text: «Пароль» (“password”) comes from French “parole” (“word”), which English borrowed too: a password is the word that lets you in. «Вайфай» is simply how Russians write “wifi”.

grammar.title: «Пароль от…»: the password to
grammar.text: «От» + genitive links a code or key to what it opens: «пароль от вайфая», «ключ от квартиры». «Вайфай» is declined like a masculine noun, so it becomes «вайфая».

pronunciation.title: Soft ль, stress on ро and фа
pronunciation.text: The final «ль» of «пароль» is a soft «л»: say pa-ROL with the tongue pressed flat against the roof of the mouth, no vowel added. «Какой» is stressed on the end: ka-KOY.

mnemonic.title: A phone that sat down
mnemonic.text: «Сел» comes from «сесть» (“to sit down”): picture your phone sinking into a chair because it has no energy left.

grammar.title: The past tense agrees in gender
grammar.text: A past verb takes the gender of its subject: «телефон» is masculine, so «сел». For a battery you would say «батарея села» (feminine -а). The person comes first with «у меня», “at me”.

pronunciation.title: Soft с in сел
pronunciation.text: The letter «е» softens the consonant before it: «сел» is “syel”, not “sel”, and «меня» sounds like mi-NYA. «Телефон» is stressed on the last syllable.

mnemonic.title: «Звонить»: a ringing bell
mnemonic.text: «Звонить» (“to call”) comes from «звон» (“a ringing”, like a bell). The prefix «пере-» adds “back”: you ring again.

grammar.title: Calling takes the dative
grammar.text: In Russian you call “to” someone, so the person after «перезвонить» is in the dative: «тебе», «вам», «ему». The perfective «перезвоню» already means “I will call back”.

pronunciation.title: Long ж in позже
pronunciation.text: «Перезвоню» ends with the stress: pee-ree-zvuh-NYOO, the «ню» soft and short. In «позже» the «зж» merges into one long «ж»: POZH-zhih.

translations.en-GB: I can't hear you very well

mnemonic.title: «Слышно»: from «слух»
mnemonic.text: «Слышно» (“audible”) shares its root with «слух» (“hearing”) and «слушать» (“to listen”). «Плохо слышно» is “badly audible”, what you say when the line is poor.

grammar.title: No subject: «слышно»
grammar.text: «Слышно» is an impersonal word meaning “it is audible”. The person you can or can't hear goes in the accusative: «тебя», or «вас» if you are formal: «Вас плохо слышно».

pronunciation.title: Flat ы, rough х
pronunciation.text: The «ы» in «слышно» is a flat, back “i”, not «и»: sluysh-nuh. The «х» in «плохо» is the rough h of Scottish “loch”.

mnemonic.title: «Обмен»: an exchange
mnemonic.text: «Обменяемся» is built on «обмен» (“exchange”): think of a currency exchange, but for phone numbers.

grammar.title: «Давай» + we: let's
grammar.text: «Давай» followed by a «мы»-form of a perfective verb means “let's”: «давай обменяемся». The thing swapped is in the instrumental: «номерами» (“with numbers”).

pronunciation.title: One stress in a long word
pronunciation.text: In «обменяемся» only «ня» is stressed: uhb-mee-NYA-yim-syuh. Squeeze the other syllables, and say the ending «-ся» as a soft “sya”.

phrases.target: Мой старший брат живёт в Лондоне

translations.en-GB: My older brother lives in London
translations.bg-BG: По-големият ми брат живее в Лондон

mnemonic.title: «Старший»: the older one
mnemonic.text: «Старший» comes from «старый» (“old”) and «младший» from «молодой» (“young”). «Брат» and “brother” are the same ancient word.

grammar.title: Older or younger
grammar.text: Russian usually says which brother or sister you mean: «старший» is older, «младший» is younger. The adjective matches the noun, so it is «старший брат» but «старшая сестра».

pronunciation.title: жи and ши are said жы, шы
pronunciation.text: After «ж» and «ш» the letter «и» is spoken as «ы»: «старший» is STAR-shuy and «живёт» is zhuy-VYOT. Both consonants are always hard, and «ё» is always stressed.

translations.bg-BG: Дъщеря ми е на пет години

mnemonic.title: Дочь is “daughter”
mnemonic.text: «Дочь» and “daughter” come from the same ancient word, which is why both start with a d.

grammar.title: Age goes in the dative
grammar.text: Russian gives age “to” the person: «моей дочери» is the dative of «моя дочь», followed by the number and «лет». After 5 you need «лет»; for 1 it is «год» and for 2 to 4 «года».

pronunciation.title: Weak vowels, soft ть
pronunciation.text: In «моей» the stress is on «ей»: muh-YAY. In «дочери» it is on «до», and the other vowels weaken. «Пять» ends in a soft «ть», with the tongue lifted: pyat'.

phrases.target: В воскресенье мы едем к бабушке

translations.en-GB: On Sunday we're going to Grandma's

mnemonic.title: Sunday: the day of rising again
mnemonic.text: «Воскресенье» (Sunday) means “resurrection”, from «воскреснуть», “to rise again”: every Sunday is a little Easter.

grammar.title: «К» + dative: to someone's
grammar.text: To go towards a person you use «к» + dative: «к бабушке» is “to Grandma's”. To be at their place you say «у» + genitive: «у бабушки».

pronunciation.title: к becomes г before б
pronunciation.text: A voiceless sound turns voiced before a voiced one: «к» before «б» sounds like «г», so «к бабушке» is g-BAH-boosh-kee. «Воскресенье» is stressed on «се»: vvuh-skree-SYEN-yuh.

translations.en-GB: My sister and I look very alike
translations.bg-BG: Със сестра ми много си приличаме

mnemonic.title: Сестра is “sister”
mnemonic.text: «Сестра» and “sister” share an ancient root, so the s-s-t sounds will carry you: sis-TRA. «Мы с» is “we with”, the Russian way of teaming up.

grammar.title: «Мы с сестрой»: my sister and I
grammar.text: «Мы с сестрой» is literally “we with sister” and means “my sister and I”. The noun after «с» is in the instrumental (-ой for feminine nouns in -а), and the adjective is plural: «похожи».

pronunciation.title: A long «с» and the stress at the end
pronunciation.text: «С сестрой» is said as one unit: the two «с» merge into a long «с», and the stress is on the last syllable: s-sis-TROY. «Очень» is stressed on «о» and ends in a soft «нь».

mnemonic.title: Дети sounds like “yeti”
mnemonic.text: «Дети» (“children”) sounds like “yeti” with a d in front: picture a yeti surrounded by a crowd of children.

grammar.title: Child and children: two words
grammar.text: The singular of «дети» is not «детя»: one child is «ребёнок». Learn the pair «ребёнок» / «дети». «У вас есть…?» is the polite “do you have…?”.

pronunciation.title: Soft т, short ending
pronunciation.text: «Есть» starts with a “y” (YEST') and ends in a soft «ть». «Дети» has a soft «т» too: the tongue lifts towards the palate, DYE-ti, and the final «и» is very short.

phrases.target: Я хочу забронировать столик на четверых

translations.en-GB: I'd like to book a table for four
translations.bg-BG: Искам да запазя маса за четирима

mnemonic.title: «Четверых»: the fourth day
mnemonic.text: «Четверых» (“four people”) is built on «четыре» (“four”), and the same root names Thursday, «четверг»: the fourth day of the Russian week.

grammar.title: «Я хочу» + infinitive
grammar.text: «Я хочу» plus an infinitive means “I want to…”: «хочу забронировать». It is not blunt in Russian: it is the normal way to say what you would like to do. «Хотеть» is irregular: «я хочу», «ты хочешь», «он хочет», but «мы хотим», «вы хотите», «они хотят».

pronunciation.title: Stress hops from word to word
pronunciation.respelling: ya khuh-CHOO zuh-bruh-NEE-ruh-vuht' STO-leek nuh chee-tvee-RUYKH
pronunciation.text: Four words carry a stress: khuh-CHOO, zuh-bruh-NEE-ruh-vuht', STO-leek and chee-tvee-RUYKH; «я» and «на» stay light. The «ч» in «хочу» and «четверых» is always soft.

phrases.target: У вас есть свободный столик на восемь?

translations.en-GB: Do you have a table free at eight?
translations.bg-BG: Имате ли свободна маса за осем часа?

mnemonic.title: Свободный: free like свобода
mnemonic.text: «Свободный» (“free, available”) comes from «свобода» (“freedom”): a free table is a table at liberty.

grammar.title: «На восемь»: for eight o'clock
grammar.text: «На» + a number names the time you book for: «на восемь» is “for eight o'clock”, with «часов» left out in speech. For eight people you would say «на восьмерых».

pronunciation.title: Flat ы, soft final ь
pronunciation.ipa: [u ˈvas ˈjesʲtʲ svɐˈbodnɨj ˈstolʲɪk nə ˈvosʲɪmʲ]
pronunciation.respelling: oo VAHS YEST' svuh-BOD-nuy STO-leek nuh VO-seem'
pronunciation.text: In «свободный» the stress is on «бод» and the ending «-ный» has a flat «ы»: svuh-BOD-nuy. «Восемь» is stressed on «во» and ends in a soft «мь».

translations.en-GB: Could we have a table on the terrace?

mnemonic.title: «Веранда»: a veranda
mnemonic.text: «Веранда» is the “veranda” you know, and in Russia it is the summer terrace of a café or restaurant. Picture your «столик» out on the veranda in the sun.

grammar.title: «На» + prepositional: at a place
grammar.text: To say where something is, Russian uses «в» or «на» with the prepositional case, whose ending is usually -е: «веранда» becomes «на веранде». Many places take «на» rather than «в»: «на веранде», «на улице», «на балконе». «Можно столик…?» (“may we have a table…?”) has no verb.

pronunciation.title: Stress on -ран-
pronunciation.text: «Веранде» is stressed on «ран»: vee-RAN-dyih. The first «е» is weak, a short “i”, and the «д» before the final «е» is soft, almost “dy”.

mnemonic.title: «Детский»: children's
mnemonic.text: «Детский» is built on «дети» (“children”), and «стульчик» is a small «стул» (“chair”): a child's little chair, the highchair.

grammar.title: «Нам нужен…»: we need
grammar.text: Russian says “to us needed…”: the people are in the dative («нам», «мне») and «нужен» agrees with the thing needed: «нужен» (m.), «нужна» (f.), «нужно» (n.), «нужны» (pl.).

pronunciation.title: тск is said цк
pronunciation.text: In «детский» the letters «тск» are pronounced «цк»: DYETS-kiy. In «стульчик» the «ль» before «ч» is soft: STOOL'-chik.

translations.en-GB: Do we need to book in advance?

mnemonic.title: Заранее: before it's early
mnemonic.text: «Заранее» is «за-» (“before”) plus «рано» (“early”): “beforehand”. «Надо» is “must”, the everyday word for what you have to do.

grammar.title: «Надо» + infinitive
grammar.text: «Надо» plus an infinitive means “one has to”: no subject is needed. The verb is imperfective («бронировать») because you ask about the general rule, not one finished booking.

pronunciation.title: Reduced vowels in «заранее»
pronunciation.text: Stress «на», «ни» and «ра»; every other «а» and «о» weakens to a short, unclear “uh”: NA-duh, bruh-NEE-ruh-vuht', zuh-RA-nee-yuh. The final «ть» of «бронировать» is soft.
